chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Not only in the world of trade, but in the world of ideas as well, our age stages ein wirklicher Ausverkauf. Everything is to be had at such a bargain price that it becomes a question whether, in the end, there is anyone who will bid. Every speculative score-keeper, who conscientiously points up the significant progress of recent philosophy — every Privatdocent, repetent, student, every emigrant and subletter in philosophy — does not stop at doubting all things, but goes further. Perhaps it would be untimely and unseasonable to inquire of them whither, in fact, they are arriving; but it is at any rate polite and modest to take it as settled that they have doubted all things, since otherwise it would be a strange way of speaking, that they went further. This preliminary movement they have, then, all of them made, and presumably so lightly that they find it unnecessary to let fall a word as to how it was done; for not even he who, anxious and concerned, sought a little instruction found such a thing — any guiding hint, any little dietetic prescription as to how one is to comport oneself under this prodigious task. “But Cartesius has done it, has he not?” Cartesius — a venerable, humble, upright thinker, whose writings, surely, no one can read without the deepest emotion — has done what he has said, and said what he has done. Alas! alas! alas! it is a great

rarity in our age! Cartesius, as he himself often enough repeats, did not doubt with respect to faith. (“Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumini naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam.” Cfr. Principia philosophiæ, pars prima §28 and §76.) He did not cry fire and make it a duty for all men to doubt, for Cartesius was a quiet, solitary thinker, not a bawling street-watchman; he modestly confessed that his method had significance only for himself and was grounded in part in his own earlier botched learning. (“Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam methodum, quam unusquisque sequi debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exponere decrevi… Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi [sc. juventutis], quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendi conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magisque detexissem.” Cfr. Dissertatio de methodo, pp. 2 and 3.) — What those ancient Greeks, who knew also somewhat of philosophy, took to be a task for an entire life, because the doubting facility is not acquired in days and weeks; what the old time-served combatant attained, who had preserved the equilibrium of doubt through every snare, who undaunted denied the certainty of sense and the certainty of thought, who incorruptibly defied the anxiety of self-love and the insinuations of sympathy — with that, in our age, every man begins.

In our age, no man stops at faith, but every man goes further. To inquire whither they arrive would perhaps be a piece of audacity; on the other hand, it is surely a sign of breeding and culture that I assume every man has faith, since otherwise it would be a strange way of speaking — that he goes further. In those ancient days it was otherwise; then faith was a task for the whole of life, because it was assumed that the believing facility is not acquired in days nor in weeks. When, then, the seasoned old man drew near to his end, having fought the good fight and kept the faith, his heart was still young enough not to have forgotten that fear and trembling which chastened the youth, which the man indeed mastered, but from which no man wholly grows away — save in so far as he should succeed in going further as early as may be. Where those venerable figures arrived, in our age every man begins, in order to go further.

The present author is by no means a philosopher; he has not comprehended the System — whether it exists, whether it is finished. He already has enough to do for his weak head with the thought of what a prodigious head every man in our age must have, since every man has such a prodigious thought. Even were one able to transpose the entire content of faith into the form of the concept, it would not follow that one had comprehended faith — comprehended how one came into it, or how it came into one. The present author is by no means a philosopher; he is, poetice et eleganter, a supplementary scribe, who neither writes the System nor promises of the System, who neither subscribes himself to the System nor signs himself over to it. He writes because for him it is a luxury, which gains in agreeableness and self-evidence the fewer there are who buy and read what he writes. He readily foresees his fate in an age that has drawn a line through passion in order to serve science — an age in which an author who would have readers must take care so to write that his book may conveniently be leafed through during the after-dinner nap, and take care to model his outward bearing after that polite gardener's apprentice in the Adresseavisen who, hat in hand and with good recommendations from the place where he last served, recommends himself to a most honored public. He foresees his fate, to be wholly ignored; he divines the more dreadful prospect that the zealous criticism will several times stand him at the school-bench; he shudders at the still more dreadful prospect that some industrious registrar, some paragraph-glutton (who, to save science, is always ready to do unto the writings of others what Trop, “to save taste,” magnanimously did unto The Destruction of the Human Race) will cut him up into §§, and do it with the same inflexibility as that man who, to serve the science of punctuation, divided his discourse by counting the words, so that fifty words made one full stop and thirty-five a semicolon. — I prostrate myself in deepest humility before every systematic peeping-Tom: “This is not the System; it has not the slightest thing to do with the System. I call down every blessing upon the System and upon the Danish shareholders in this Omnibus — for a tower, indeed, it will scarcely become. I wish them all and every one of them luck and benediction.”

Most respectfully,
Johannes de silentio.

chapters.title: Exordium
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a man who, as a child, had heard that beautiful tale of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and a second time received a son against expectation. When he grew older, he read the same tale with still greater wonder; for life had divided what had been united in the child's pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thought turned to that tale; his enthusiasm waxed stronger and stronger, and yet less and less could he understand the tale. At last he forgot all else for its sake; his soul had but one wish — to see Abraham — and one longing, to have been a witness of that event. His desire was not to behold the beautiful regions of the Orient, not the earthly glory of the promised land, not that god-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, not the venerable figure of the aged patriarch, not the vigorous youth of Isaac whom God bestowed — he had nothing against its all taking place upon a barren heath. His craving was to accompany them on the three days' journey, when Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be present in the hour when Abraham lifted up his eye and saw the mountain of Moriah in the distance, the hour when he left the asses behind and went on alone with Isaac up to the mountain; for what occupied him was not the artistic weaving of the imagination, but the shudder of thought.

That man was no thinker; he felt no need to come out beyond faith. It seemed to him that it must be the most glorious thing to be remembered as its father, an enviable lot to possess it, even though no one knew it.
That man was no learned exegete; he knew no Hebrew. Had he known Hebrew, he might perhaps easily have understood the tale of Abraham.

“And God tempted Abraham and said unto him: Take Isaac, thine only son, whom thou lovest, and go thou into the land of Moriah, and offer him there for a burnt offering upon a mountain which I will show thee.”

It was an early morning. Abraham rose betimes; he had the asses saddled, left his tent, and Isaac with him; but Sarah looked out of the window after them, down through the valley, until she saw them no more. They rode in silence for three days; on the morning of the fourth day Abraham still spoke not a word, but lifted up his eye and saw Mount Moriah in the distance. He left the lads behind and went on alone, with Isaac by the hand, up to the mountain. But Abraham said to himself: “I will not, however, conceal from Isaac whither this journey is leading him.” He stood still; he laid his hand upon Isaac's head in blessing, and Isaac bowed himself to receive it. And Abraham's countenance was that of a father, his glance was mild, his speech admonishing. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be uplifted; he clasped Abraham's knees, he made supplication at his foot, he pleaded for his young life, for his fair hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham's house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the lad up and walked on with him by the hand, and his words were full of consolation and admonition. But Isaac could not understand him. He climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac understood him not. Then he turned away from him for a moment; but when Isaac the second time saw Abraham's countenance, it was changed: his glance was wild, his form was terror. He seized Isaac by the breast, he cast him to the ground, and said: “Foolish lad, believest thou that I am thy father? I am an idolater. Believest thou that this is God's command? No, it is my own pleasure.” Then Isaac trembled and cried out in his anguish: “God in heaven, have mercy upon me; God of Abraham, have mercy upon me; if I have no father upon earth, then be Thou my father!” But Abraham said softly within himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank Thee; it is, after all, better that he should believe me an inhuman wretch than that he should lose his faith in Thee.”

When the child is to be weaned, the mother blackens her breast — for it were indeed a shame that the breast should still appear lovely when the child must no longer have it. So the child believes that the breast has been changed, but the mother is the same; her gaze is loving and tender as ever. Happy he who needed no more dreadful means to wean the child!

It was an early morning. Abraham rose betimes; he embraced Sarah, the bride of his old age, and Sarah kissed Isaac, who had taken away her shame, who was her pride, her hope in all generations. So they rode silently along the way, and Abraham's gaze was fixed upon the ground, until on the fourth day he lifted up his eye and saw Mount Moriah far off; but his gaze turned again toward the ground. In silence he laid the wood in order; in silence he bound Isaac; in silence he drew the knife — then he saw the ram which God had appointed. He sacrificed it and went home. — — — From that day on, Abraham was old; he could not forget that God had required this of him. Isaac throve as before; but Abraham's eye was darkened, he saw joy no more.

It was an early morning. Abraham rose betimes; he kissed Sarah, the young mother, and Sarah kissed Isaac, her delight, her joy in all times. And Abraham rode pensively along the way; he thought of Hagar and of the son whom he had driven out into the wilderness. He climbed Mount Moriah, he drew the knife.

It was a quiet evening when Abraham rode out alone, and he rode toward Mount Moriah; he cast himself upon his face, he prayed God to forgive him his sin, that he had been willing to sacrifice Isaac, that the father had forgotten his duty toward the son. Often did he ride his solitary way, but he had no peace. He could not conceive that it was a sin, that he had been willing to offer up to God the best he possessed, that for which he himself would gladly have laid down his life many times over; and if it was a sin, if he had not so loved Isaac, then he could not understand that it could ever be forgiven — for what sin was more terrible?

It was an early morning. Everything was made ready for the journey in Abraham's house. He took leave of Sarah; and Eliezer, the faithful servant, accompanied him out upon the way, until he turned back again. They rode in accord together, Abraham and Isaac, until they came to Mount Moriah. But Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calm and gentle; yet as he turned aside and drew the knife, Isaac saw that Abraham's left hand clenched itself in despair, that a shudder went through his body — but Abraham drew the knife.

Then they returned home again, and Sarah hastened to meet them; but Isaac had lost his faith. There has never in all the world been a word said of it, and Isaac never spoke to any man of what he had seen, and Abraham did not divine that any man had seen it.
When the child is to be weaned, the mother has a stronger food at hand, that the child may not perish. Happy he who has the stronger food at hand.

Thus, and in many similar ways, did that man of whom we speak meditate upon this event. Each time, when after a wandering to Mount Moriah he returned home, he sank down with weariness, folded his hands, and said: “Yet no one was so great as Abraham; who is able to understand him?”

chapters.title: Eulogy on Abraham
paragraphs: Were there no eternal consciousness in a man, were there at the bottom of all things only a wildly fermenting power which, writhing in dark passions, brought forth everything great and everything insignificant, were a bottomless emptiness, never satisfied, hidden beneath all — what then were life but despair? Were it so, were there no holy bond binding humankind together, were the one generation to spring up after the other as the leaves of the forest, were the one generation to succeed the other as the song of birds in the wood, were the race to pass through the world as the ship goes through the sea, as the wind through the desert, a thoughtless and unfruitful labor; were an eternal forgetfulness, ever hungry, lying in wait for its prey, and there no power strong enough to wrest it from her — how empty then and comfortless were life! But for that very reason it is not so; and as God created man and woman, so He fashioned the hero and the poet or orator. The latter can do nothing of what the former does; he can only admire, love, rejoice in the hero. Yet is he too happy, not less than the hero; for the hero is, as it were, his better being, with which he is enamored, glad that it is not, after all, himself, that his love can be admiration. He is the genius of remembrance, can do nothing but remind men of what has been done, do nothing but admire what has been done; he takes nothing of his own, but is jealous of what has been entrusted to him. He follows his heart's choice; but when he has found what he sought, then he wanders about at every man's door with his song and with his speech, that all may admire the hero as he does, may be proud of the hero as he is. This is his exploit, his humble task, this is his faithful service in the house of the hero. If he thus remains true to his love, if he strives day and night with the guile of forgetfulness, which would lure the hero away from him, then has he accomplished his work, then is he united with the hero, who has loved him just as faithfully; for the poet is, as it were, the hero's better being — feeble indeed, as a remembrance is, but also transfigured, as a remembrance is. Therefore shall no man be forgotten who was great; and though it tarry never so long, though the cloud of misunderstanding take the hero away, his lover yet comes; and the longer the time has gone, the more faithfully does he cleave to him.

No! none shall be forgotten who was great in the world; but every one was great in his own way, and every one in proportion to the greatness of that which he loved. For he who loved himself was great by himself, and he who loved other men was great by his devotion; but he who loved God was greater than all. Every one shall be remembered; but every one became great in proportion to his expectation. One man became great by expecting the possible, another by expecting the eternal; but he who expected the impossible was greater than all. Every one shall be remembered; but every one was great in proportion to the magnitude of that with which he strove. For he who strove with the world became great by overcoming the world, and he who strove with himself became greater by overcoming himself; but he who strove with God was greater than all. Thus was there strife in the world, man against man, one against

a thousand; but he who strove with God was greater than all. Thus was there strife upon earth: there was he who overcame all by his strength, and there was he who overcame God by his powerlessness. There was he who relied upon himself and won all; there was he who, secure in his strength, sacrificed all; but he who believed God was greater than all. There was he who was great by his strength, and he who was great by his wisdom, and he who was great by his hope, and he who was great by his love; but Abraham was greater than all — great by that strength whose strength is powerlessness, great by that wisdom whose secret is folly, great by that hope whose form is madness, great by that love which is hatred of self.

By faith Abraham went forth out of the land of his fathers, and became a stranger in the land of promise. One thing he left behind, one thing he took with him: he left his earthly understanding behind, and took faith with him; otherwise he would surely not have gone forth, but had thought, “It is unreasonable.” By faith he was a stranger in the land of promise, and there was nothing to remind him of what was dear; but everything, by its newness, tempted his soul to a wistful longing. And yet was he God's chosen, in whom the Lord had His pleasure! Yea, had he been an outcast, thrust away from God's grace, he might better have grasped it; as it was, it was as a mockery upon him and upon his faith. There was in the world also one who lived banished from the fatherland which he loved. He is not forgotten, neither his lamentations, when in wistfulness he sought and found what was lost. Of Abraham there is no lamentation. It is human to lament, human to weep with the weeper, but it is greater to believe, more blessed to behold the believer. By faith Abraham received the promise, that in his seed all the generations of the earth should be blessed. Time went on, the possibility was there; Abraham believed. Time went on, it became unreasonable; Abraham believed. There was, in the world, also one who had an expectation. Time went on, it drew toward evening; he was not so wretched as to have forgotten his expectation, therefore shall he not be forgotten either. Then he grieved, and grief did not deceive him as life had done; it did for him all that it could, and in the sweetness of grief he possessed his disappointed expectation. It is human to grieve, it is human to grieve with the griever; but it is greater to believe, more blessed to behold the believer. Of Abraham we have no song of mourning. He did not mournfully count the days as the times went on; he did not look upon Sarah with suspicious glances, lest she should grow old; he did not stop the course of the sun, that Sarah should not age and with her his expectation; he did not soothingly sing for Sarah his wistful lay. Abraham grew old, Sarah was mocked in the land; and yet was he God's chosen and heir of the promise, that in his seed all the generations of the earth should be blessed. Were it not better, then, that he had not been God's chosen? What is it to be God's chosen? Is it to be denied in youth the wish of youth, that with great trouble it may be fulfilled in old age? But Abraham believed, and held the promise fast. Had Abraham wavered, then had he given it up. He would have said unto God: “Then perhaps it is not Thy will after all that it should come to pass; then will I give up the wish; it was my only one, it was my blessedness. My soul is sincere; I harbor no secret resentment because Thou hast denied it.” He would not have been forgotten; he would have rescued many by his example, yet would not have become the father of faith. For it is great to give up one's wish, but it is greater to hold fast to it after having given it up; it is great to lay hold of the eternal, but it is greater to hold fast to the temporal after having given it up. — Then came the fullness of time. Had Abraham not believed, then perhaps Sarah had died of sorrow, and Abraham, dulled by grief, had not understood the fulfillment, but smiled at it as at a dream of youth. But Abraham believed, therefore was he young; for he who ever hopes for the best grows old, deceived by life, and he who is ever prepared for the worst grows old early; but he who believes preserves an eternal youth. Praised therefore be that tale! For Sarah, though stricken in years, was young enough to long for a mother's joy, and Abraham, though grey-haired, was young enough to wish to be a father. Outwardly, the wonder lies in this, that it came to pass according to their expectation; in a deeper sense, the wonder of faith lies in this, that Abraham and Sarah were young enough to wish, and that faith had preserved their wish, and therewith their youth. He received the fulfillment of the promise; he received it believing, and it came to pass according to the promise and according to faith — for Moses smote the rock with his staff, but he believed not.
Then was there joy in Abraham's house, when Sarah stood as bride upon the day of the golden wedding.

Yet so was it not to remain; once again was Abraham to be tried. He had striven with that cunning power which invents all things, with that watchful foe who never slumbers, with that old man who outlives all things — he had striven with time, and had kept the faith. Now was all the dread of the strife gathered into a single moment. “And God tempted Abraham, and said unto him: Take Isaac, thine only son, whom thou lovest, and go thou into the land of Moriah, and offer him there for a burnt offering upon a mountain which I will show thee.”

Then was all forfeited, more dreadful than if it had never been! So the Lord was only making sport of Abraham! Wonderfully had He made the unreasonable actual; now would He see it again brought to nought. It was a folly, but Abraham did not laugh at it as did Sarah when the promise was proclaimed. All was forfeited! seventy years of faithful expectation, the brief joy of faith's

fulfillment. Who, then, is he who plucks the staff from the old man? Who is he who demands that he himself shall break it? Who is he who renders comfortless the grey hairs of a man? Who is he who demands that he himself shall make them so? Is there no compassion for the venerable old man, none for the innocent child? And yet was Abraham God's chosen, and it was the Lord who laid the trial upon him. All should now be forfeited! the glorious memory of the race, the promise in Abraham's seed — it was but a passing fancy, a fleeting thought which the Lord had had, and which Abraham was now to efface. That glorious treasure, as old as faith in Abraham's heart, many, many years older than Isaac, the fruit of Abraham's life, sanctified by prayers, ripened in struggles — the blessing upon Abraham's lips, this fruit was now to be plucked unseasonably, and to remain without meaning; for what meaning had it, when Isaac was to be sacrificed? That wistful, yet blessed hour, when Abraham was to take leave of all that was dear to him, when once more he was to lift up his venerable head, when his countenance was to shine like the Lord's, when he was to gather his whole soul into a blessing mighty enough to make Isaac blessed all his days — this hour should not come! For Abraham was indeed to take leave of Isaac, yet in such wise that he himself should remain behind; death should part them, yet in such wise that Isaac should be its prey. The old man was not gladly in death to lay his blessing hand upon Isaac, but, weary of life, was to lay a violent hand upon Isaac. And it was God who tried him. Yea, woe! woe to the messenger who had come before Abraham with such tidings! Who had dared to be this envoy of sorrow? But it was God who tried Abraham.

Yet Abraham believed, and believed for this life. Yea, had his faith been only for a life to come, then had he the more lightly cast all aside, to hasten out of the world to which he did not belong. But Abraham's faith was not such — if such there be; for properly it is not faith, but the remotest possibility of faith, which on the utmost edge of the horizon descries its object, yet is separated from it by a yawning abyss within which despair plies its game. But Abraham believed precisely for this life: that he should grow old in the land, honored among the people, blessed in his progeny, unforgettable in Isaac — his dearest in life, whom he embraced with a love for which it was but a poor expression to say that he faithfully fulfilled the father's duty to love the son, as it sounds also in the divine charge: the son whom thou lovest. Jacob had twelve sons, and one whom he loved; Abraham had only one, and him he loved.

But Abraham believed and doubted not; he believed the unreasonable. Had Abraham doubted — then had he done something else, something great and glorious; for how could Abraham do anything but what is great and glorious? He had gone forth unto Mount Moriah, he had cleft the wood, he had kindled the pile, he had drawn the knife — he had cried unto God: “Despise not this offering; it is not the best I possess, that I know well; for what is an old man against the child of the promise? But it is the best I can give Thee. Let Isaac never come to know it, that he may comfort himself with his youth.” He would have plunged the knife into his own breast. He would have been admired in the world, and his name not forgotten; but it is one thing to be admired, another to become a guiding star which saves the troubled soul.
But Abraham believed. He did not pray for himself, that he might move the Lord; it was only when the just punishment went forth upon Sodom and Gomorrah that Abraham came forward with his entreaties.
We read in those holy Scriptures: “And God tempted Abraham, and said: Abraham, Abraham, where art thou?

but Abraham answered: Here am I.” Thou to whom my speech is addressed, was it so with thee? When far off thou sawest the heavy dispensations drawing nigh, didst thou not say to the mountains, “Hide me!”, to the hills, “Fall upon me!”? Or wert thou stronger? Yet did not thy foot move slowly along the way? did it not, as it were, long backward toward the old paths? When thou wert called, didst thou answer? or didst thou not answer, and that perhaps softly, in a whisper? Not so Abraham: gladly, blithely, trustingly, with a loud voice he answered: Here am I. We read further: “And Abraham rose betimes in the morning.” As though it were to a feast, so did he hasten; and betimes in the morning he was upon the appointed place, upon Mount Moriah. He spake nothing to Sarah, nothing to Eliezer; for who, after all, could understand him? Had not the temptation, by its very nature, taken from him the pledge of silence? “He cleft the wood, he bound Isaac, he kindled the pile, he drew the knife.” My hearer! There has been many a father who believed that in his child he was losing what was dearest to him in the world, that he was being deprived of every hope of the future; but there was no one who in that sense was the child of the promise, as Isaac was for Abraham. There has been many a father who lost his child, but then it was God, the unalterable and inscrutable will of the Almighty — His hand took it. Not so with Abraham. For him a heavier trial was reserved, and Isaac's fate was, with the knife, laid in Abraham's hand. And there he stood, the old man with his only hope! But he doubted not; he looked not anxiously to right or left; he did not challenge heaven by his prayers. He knew that it was God the Almighty who tried him; he knew it was the heaviest sacrifice that could be required of him; but he knew also that no sacrifice is too heavy, when God requires it — and he drew the knife.

Who strengthened Abraham's arm? who held up his right hand, that it might not sink down powerless? Whoso looks upon this is stricken with palsy. Who strengthened Abraham's soul, that the eye of him grew not dark, so that he saw neither Isaac nor the ram? Whoso looks upon this is stricken blind. — And yet rare enough perhaps is he who is stricken with palsy or with blindness; rarer still he who worthily tells what came to pass. We all of us know it — it was only a trial.

Had Abraham, when he stood upon Mount Moriah, doubted; had he, perplexed, looked about him; had he, before he drew the knife, by chance discovered the ram; had God allowed him to offer it up instead of Isaac — then had he gone home, all had been as before, he had Sarah, he kept Isaac, and yet how altered! For his retreat had been a flight, his deliverance an accident, his reward shame, his future perhaps perdition. He had then borne witness neither to his faith nor to God's grace, but only to how dreadful a thing it is to journey up to Mount Moriah. Then would Abraham not be forgotten, neither Mount Moriah. Then would it be named — not as Ararat, where the ark came to rest, but as a place of horror, because there it was that Abraham doubted.

Venerable Father Abraham! When thou camest home from Mount Moriah, thou hadst no need of any eulogy to comfort thee for what was lost; for thou didst gain all, and didst keep Isaac, was it not so? The Lord took him from thee no more, but thou didst sit gladly at the board with him in thy tent, as thou dost yonder through all eternities. Venerable Father Abraham! Millennia have rolled away since those days, yet thou hast no need of any late lover to wrest thy memory from the violence of forgetfulness; for every tongue remembers thee — and yet thou rewardest thy lover more gloriously than any other; thou makest him blessed yonder in thy

bosom; thou holdest fast here his eye and his heart by the wonder of thy deed. Venerable Father Abraham! Second father of the race! Thou who didst first apprehend, and bear witness to, that prodigious passion which disdains the dreadful strife with the raging of the elements and with the powers of creation in order to strive with God; thou who didst first know that highest passion, the holy, pure, and humble expression of that divine madness which was admired even by the heathen — forgive him who would speak unto thy praise, if he should not do it aright. He spake humbly, as it was his heart's desire; he spake briefly, as is fitting; but he shall never forget that thou didst need a hundred years to obtain, against expectation, a son of thy old age, that thou hadst to draw the knife before thou keptest Isaac; he shall never forget that in a hundred and thirty years thou camest no further than to faith.

chapters.title: Preliminary Expectoration
paragraphs: An old saying, drawn from the outward and visible world, runs: “only he who works gets the bread.” Strangely enough, the saying does not fit the world to which it most properly belongs; for the outward world is subject to the law of imperfection, and there it happens again and again that he too who does not work gets the bread, that he who sleeps gets it more abundantly than he who works. In the outward world, all things belong to the holder; that world is enslaved beneath the law of indifference, and the spirit of the ring obeys him who has the ring, be he a Noureddin or an Aladdin; and he who has the treasures of the world has them, no matter how he came by them. In the world of the spirit it is otherwise. There an eternal divine order rules; there it does not rain alike upon the just and the unjust, there the sun does not shine alike upon the good and the evil; there it holds true that only he who works gets the bread, only he who was in anguish finds rest, only he who descends into the underworld saves the beloved, only he who draws the knife gets Isaac. He who will not work gets no bread, but is deceived, as the gods deceived Orpheus with an airy figure in place of the beloved — deceived him because he was effeminate, not manly, deceived him because he was a cithara-player, not a man. Here it does not avail to have Abraham for father, or seventeen ancestors; he who will not work, to him fits that which is written of the daughters of Israel — he brings forth wind; but he who will work, he brings forth his own father.

There is a knowledge which presumes to introduce into the world of the spirit that same law of indifference under which the outward world groans. It supposes it enough to know what is great; no further work is needed. But for that very reason it does not get the bread; it perishes of hunger, while everything is being changed into gold. And what does it know, after all? In the contemporary days of Greece there were many thousands, in later generations innumerable, who knew all the triumphs of Miltiades; but there was only one whom they made sleepless. There were countless generations who knew word for word, by heart, the tale of Abraham; how many did it make sleepless?

The story of Abraham has now this remarkable property, that it always remains glorious, however poorly one may understand it; yet here too it holds, that one must be willing to work and to be burdened. But men will not work, and yet they would understand the story. They speak in praise of Abraham, but how? They give the whole an altogether ordinary expression: “the great thing was that he so loved God that he was willing to sacrifice unto Him the best.” It is very true; but “the best” is an indefinite expression. In the rush of thought and tongue one quite securely identifies Isaac and the best, and the meditator may comfortably puff at his pipe during the meditation, and the hearer may comfortably stretch out his legs. Had that rich young man whom Christ met upon his way sold all his goods and given to the poor, then should we praise him, as we praise all that is great, and not even understand him without effort; yet he had not for that become an Abraham, although he sacrificed the best. What is left out of Abraham's history is the anguish; for to money I have no ethical obligation, but to the son the father has the highest and most sacred. Yet anguish is a perilous thing for the soft of heart, and so they forget it, and notwithstanding that they would speak of Abraham. They speak then, and in the course of speech the two expressions, Isaac and the best, change places; all goes excellently. Should it, however, fall out that there were among the hearers a man who suffered from sleeplessness, then the most dreadful, the deepest, the tragic and comic misunderstanding lies very near at hand. He went home, he would do as Abraham did; for the son is, after all, the best. If that orator came to know of it, he would perhaps go to him; he would gather all his clerical dignity and cry out: “abominable man, refuse of society, what devil hath so possessed thee that thou wouldst murder thy son?” And the priest, who had felt no warmth nor perspiration in preaching about Abraham, marveled at himself, at the wrath of earnestness with which he thundered down upon that wretched man; he was glad in himself, for he had never spoken with such pith and unction; he said unto himself and unto his wife: “I am an orator; what was lacking was the occasion. When I preached on Sunday about Abraham, I felt myself not in the least seized.” Had this same orator a small surplus of understanding to be shed, then I think he would have shed it, if the sinner had quietly and with dignity replied: that, surely, was what thou thyself didst preach about on Sunday. How indeed should the priest get such a thing into his head? — and yet so it was, the only fault being that he had not known what he was saying. That there is, after all, no poet who could resolve to prefer such situations to the trumpery and tinsel with which men fill comedies and romances! The comic and the tragic touch one another here in absolute infinity. The priest's discourse was perhaps in itself ridiculous enough, but became infinitely ridiculous in its effect, and yet the effect was quite natural. Or, if the sinner without raising any objection were really converted by the priest's chastening rebuke; if this zealous cleric went home glad, glad in the consciousness that he wrought not only from the pulpit, but, above all, with irresistible power as a curer of souls; that on the Sunday he had inspired the congregation, while on the Monday, like a cherub with flaming sword, he set himself before the man who by his deed would have put to shame that old saying, that things do not go in the world as the priest preaches *.

If, on the contrary, the sinner was not convinced, then his situation is tragic enough. He was then presumably executed or sent to the madhouse; in short, he became unhappy in respect of so-called actuality; in another sense, however, I think Abraham made him happy; for he who works does not perish.

How does one explain such a contradiction as that of yonder orator? Is it because Abraham has acquired a prescriptive right to be a great man, so that what he does is great, and when another does the same it is sin, sin crying to heaven? In that case I have no wish to take part in such thoughtless eulogizing. If faith cannot make it a holy act to be willing to murder one's son, then let the same judgment go forth upon Abraham as upon every other. Does one perhaps lack the courage to carry one's thought through, to say that Abraham was a murderer, then it is surely better to acquire that courage than to waste time on undeserved panegyrics. The ethical expression for what Abraham did is, that he was willing to murder Isaac; the *( In the old days they used to say: it is sad that things do not go in the world as the priest preaches — perhaps the time will come, especially with the help of philosophy, when one shall be able to say: happily, things do not go as the priest preaches; for in life there is at least a little sense, in his sermon there is none at all.

religious expression is, that he was willing to sacrifice Isaac; but in this very contradiction lies the anguish, which can well make a man sleepless, and yet Abraham is not who he is without this anguish. Or did Abraham perhaps not do at all what is told, was it perhaps, by reason of the conditions of those times, something quite different — then let us forget him; for what is the use of remembering that past which cannot become a present? Or had perhaps yonder orator forgotten somewhat, that corresponded to the ethical forgetfulness, that Isaac was the son? For when faith, by being made into Nichts and a nullity, is taken away, there remains only the raw fact, that Abraham was willing to murder Isaac, which is easy enough for any man to imitate who has not the faith — that is, that faith which makes it hard for him.

I, for my part, do not lack the courage to think a thought to the end; hitherto I have feared none, and should I encounter such a one, I trust I shall at least have the sincerity to say, this thought I fear, it stirs up something else within me, and therefore I will not think it; if I do wrong therein, the punishment will surely not fail. Had I recognized it as the verdict of truth that Abraham was a murderer, I know not whether I could have brought my piety toward him to silence. Had I, however, thought it, I should presumably have kept silent thereon; for in such thoughts a man is not to initiate others. But Abraham is no phantom; he has not slept his way to renown, he owes it not to a caprice of fortune.

Can one then speak unreservedly of Abraham, without running the risk that some single individual go astray and do likewise? Dare I not, then will I altogether keep silence about Abraham, and above all I will not so debase him that he becomes thereby a snare for the weak. For if one make faith all in all — that is, what it is — then I think one may speak without danger thereof in our age, which scarce extravagates in faith; and it is only by faith that one comes to resemble Abraham, not by murder. If one make love a fleeting mood, a voluptuous stirring in a man, then one but lays snares for the weak, when one would speak of love's exploits. A passing emotion, indeed, hath every man; but if for that reason every man would do the dreadful thing which love hath consecrated as an immortal deed, then all is lost, both the deed and the deluded one. One could, then, well speak of Abraham; for the great can never harm, when it is apprehended in its greatness; it is as a two-edged sword, that slayeth and saveth. If the lot fell upon me to speak thereof, I would begin by showing what a pious and god-fearing man Abraham was, worthy to be called God's chosen. Only such a one is laid under such a trial; but who is such a one? Next would I depict how Abraham loved Isaac. To that end would I beseech all good spirits to stand by me, that my discourse might become as glowing as fatherly love is. I hope then to be able to depict it in such wise that there were not many a father in the king's realms and lands who durst maintain that he loved thus. But if he loved not as Abraham, then was every thought of sacrificing Isaac a temptation. Of this one might already speak for several Sundays — there is no need to be hasty. The consequence would then be, were it rightly spoken of, that some fathers would not at all desire to hear more, but would for the time being be glad if it really succeeded with them to love as Abraham loved. Were there, then, one who, having heard the great, but also the dreadful in Abraham's deed, dared to set forth upon the way, then would I saddle my horse and ride with him. At every station, until we came to Mount Moriah, would I explain to him that he could yet turn back, could repent the misunderstanding that he was called to be tried in such a strife, could confess that he lacked the courage, so that God Himself must take Isaac, if He would have him. It is my conviction that such a man is not cast off, that he can be made blessed with all the others, but in time he becomes not so. Would one not, even in the most believing ages, have judged thus of such a man? I have known a man who could once have saved my life, had he been magnanimous. He said straight out: “I see well enough what I might do; but I dare not, I fear that I shall hereafter lack strength, that I shall regret it.” He was not magnanimous; but who therefore would not still continue to love him?

When I had thus spoken, when I had so moved the hearers that they had at least become aware of the dialectical strivings of faith and its gigantic passion, then would I not bring upon myself an error on the side of the hearers, that they should think: “he hath now faith in so high a degree, for us it is enough to hold by his coat-tails.” For I would add: “I have by no means the faith. By nature I am a shrewd head, and every such

” head hath always great difficulties in making the movement of faith, without my, however, in and for itself ascribing any value to that difficulty which carried the shrewd head further by overcoming it than to the point at which the simplest and most innocent
person more easily arrives.”

Yet love hath in the poets her priests, and now and then one heareth a voice that knoweth how to maintain her in honor; but of faith no word is heard — who speaketh in praise of this passion? Philosophy goeth further. Theology sitteth painted at the window and woos its favor, offering its loveliness for sale to philosophy. It is said to be hard to understand Hegel, but to understand Abraham — that is a small matter. To go beyond Hegel, that is a marvel; but to go beyond Abraham, that is the easiest thing of all. I, for my part, have

spent considerable time in trying to understand Hegelian philosophy, believe also that I have in some measure understood it, am bold enough to think that, when I, despite all the pains taken, in certain places cannot understand him, then he himself was probably not quite clear. All this I do easily, naturally; my head suffers not therefrom. When, on the other hand, I am to set about thinking upon Abraham, then am I as one annihilated. At every moment I catch sight of yonder prodigious paradox, which is the content of Abraham's life; at every moment I am thrust back, and my thought, for all its passion, cannot penetrate it, cannot come a hair's-breadth further. I strain every muscle to win the prospect; in that same instant I am paralyzed.

I am not unacquainted with what hath been admired in the world as great and high-minded; my soul feeleth its kinship therewith, is in all humility assured that it was also my cause for which the hero strove; in the moment of beholding I cry to myself: jam tua res agitur. Into the hero I can think myself; into Abraham I cannot think myself; when I have reached the height, I fall down, since that which is offered me is a paradox. Yet by no means do I therefore mean that faith is some lowly thing; on the contrary, that it is the highest, and that it is dishonest of philosophy to put something else in its place and to make light of faith. Philosophy can not and shall not give faith; but it shall understand itself, and know what it offers, and take nothing away — least of all wheedle men out of something, as though it were nothing. I am not unacquainted with the necessities and dangers of life; I fear them not, and go cheerfully to meet them. I am not unfamiliar with the dreadful; my memory is a faithful wife, and my fancy is, what I myself am not, a busy little maid, who sitteth still all day at her work, and in the evening knoweth how to chatter so prettily for me, that I must look thereon, although it is not always landscapes, or flowers, or shepherd-tales that she paints. I have looked it in the face, I flee it not in fear; but I know full well, that, though I go to meet it manfully, my courage is yet not the courage of faith and is nothing to compare therewith. I cannot make the movement of faith; I cannot shut mine eyes and plunge trustingly into the absurd; that is to me an impossibility, but I do not boast of it. I am persuaded that God is love; this thought hath for me an original lyrical validity. When it is present unto me, I am unutterably blessed; when it is absent, I long for it more vehemently than the lover for his object; but I do not believe — this courage I lack. God's love is to me, both in the direct and the inverse sense, incommensurable for the whole of actuality. I am not coward enough to whimper and complain on that account, but neither am I sly enough to deny that faith is something far higher. I can well endure to live in my own fashion; I am glad and content, but my joy is not the joy of faith, and is, in comparison with that, unhappy. I burden not God with my little sorrows; the particular concerns me not; I gaze only upon my love, and keep its virginal flame pure and clear; faith is persuaded that God concerneth Himself about the smallest thing. I am content in this life to be wedded with the left hand; faith is humble enough to ask the right; for that this is humility I deny not, and shall never deny.

Is, then, every man in my generation truly able to make the movements of faith? If I have not greatly mistaken him, he is rather inclined to be proud of doing what he does not even believe me capable of, that is — the imperfect. It goes against my soul to do what so often happens, to speak inhumanly of the great, as though some thousands of years were a prodigious distance; I prefer to speak humanly thereof, as if it had happened yesterday, and let only greatness itself be the distance, which either uplifts or judges. If, then, I (in the quality of a tragic hero, for higher I cannot rise) had been summoned to such an extraordinary king's progress as that to Mount Moriah, I know well what I should have done. I had not been coward enough to remain at home, neither had I lain idling on the high road, neither had I forgotten the knife, that there might be a little hindrance; I am tolerably assured that I should have been on the stroke of the hour, had everything in order — perhaps rather had come too early, that the thing might soon be over. But I know also what further I should have done. In the same moment as I mounted the horse, I should have said unto myself: now is all lost, God demandeth Isaac, I sacrifice him, and with him all my joy — yet is God love, and remaineth so for me; for in temporality God and I cannot speak together, we have no language in common. Perhaps in our age there will be some one or other foolish enough, envious enough of the great, to wish to persuade himself and me that, if I had really done this, I should have done a yet greater thing than what Abraham did; for my prodigious resignation was far more ideal and poetical than Abraham's pettiness. And yet this is the greatest of untruths; for my prodigious resignation was the surrogate for faith. I could not then do more than the infinite movement, in order to find myself, and again to rest in myself. Neither had I then loved Isaac as Abraham loved. That I was resolute to make the movement might prove my courage, humanly speaking; that I loved him with my whole soul is the presupposition, without which the whole becomes a misdeed; but I loved not even as Abraham; for then had I held back even at the last minute, without therefore coming too late upon Mount Moriah. I had moreover, by my conduct, marred the whole history; for if I had received Isaac again, then had I been in embarrassment. What fell easiest to Abraham, would fall hard to me — to be glad again at Isaac! For he who, with the whole infinity of his soul, proprio motu et propriis auspiciis, hath made the infinite movement, and can do no more, he keepeth Isaac only in pain.

But what did Abraham? He came neither too early nor too late. He mounted the ass, he rode slowly along the way. In all that time he believed; he believed that God would not require Isaac of him, while yet he was willing to sacrifice him, when it should be demanded. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for of human reckoning there could be no question, and it was indeed the absurd that God, who required it of him, should in the next moment recall the demand. He climbed the mountain; even in that moment when the knife flashed, he believed — that God would not require Isaac. He was, indeed, surprised by the issue, but through a double movement he had attained his first state, and therefore received Isaac more gladly than the first time. Let us go further. Let us suppose Isaac really was sacrificed. Abraham believed. He believed not that he should once be blessed yonder, but that he should be made happy here in this world. God could give him a new Isaac, could call the sacrificed one to life again. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for all human reckoning had long since ceased. That sorrow can make a man mad, that one sees, and it is heavy enough; that there is a will-power that can luff so close to the wind that it saves the understanding, although the man becomes a little odd, that one sees also; I purpose not to belittle it; but to be able to lose one's understanding, and with it the whole of finitude, of which it is the broker, and then by virtue of the absurd to win precisely that same finitude — this affrights my soul; but I therefore say not that it is a lowly thing, since on the contrary it is the only marvel. The common opinion is that what faith brings forth is no work of art, that it is coarse and clumsy work, only for the more uncouth natures; yet it is far otherwise. The dialectic of faith is the finest and most remarkable of all; it hath an elevation of which I can well form a conception, but no more. I can make the great springboard-leap, whereby I pass over into infinity; my back is as a rope-dancer's, twisted in my childhood, therefore it falleth easy to me — I can, one, two, three, go upon my head into existence; but the next thing I cannot do; for the marvelous I cannot do, but only marvel at. Yea, had Abraham, in the moment he swung his leg over the ass's back, said unto himself: now is Isaac lost, I might just as well sacrifice him here at home as travel the long way to Moriah — then I have no need of Abraham, whereas I now bow myself seven times before his name and seventy times before his deed. For this hath he not done, which I can prove from the fact that he was glad to receive Isaac, right inwardly glad, that he had need of no preparation, no time to gather himself upon finitude and its joy. Were it not so with Abraham, then had he perhaps loved God, but not believed; for he who loveth God without faith, reflecteth upon himself; he who loveth God in faith, reflecteth upon God.

Upon this peak standeth Abraham. The last stage which he loseth from sight is the infinite resignation. He goeth in truth further and cometh to faith; for all those caricatures of faith, the wretched lukewarm sluggishness which thinketh: there is no danger, it is not worth grieving before the time; the miserable hope which saith: one cannot know what shall happen, it might still be possible — these caricatures belong at home in the wretchedness of life, and them already the infinite resignation hath infinitely despised.

Abraham I cannot understand; in a certain sense I can learn nothing from him, save to marvel. When one supposeth that by considering the issue of yonder history one should be moved to believe, then one deceiveth oneself, and would defraud God of the first movement of faith; one would suck life-wisdom out of the paradox. Perhaps it succeedeth with one or another; for our age stoppeth not at faith, not at her miracle of turning water into wine; she goeth further, she turneth wine into water.

Were it not, after all, best to stop at faith, and is it not revolting that every man wisheth to go further? When in our age — and this is proclaimed in various ways — men will not stop at love, whither do they then come? To earthly cleverness, petty calculation, to wretchedness and misery, to all that can make man's divine origin doubtful. Were it not better that one stopped at faith, and that he who standeth take heed lest he fall; for the movement of faith must constantly be made by virtue of the absurd, yet, well to be marked, in such wise that one loseth not finitude, but winneth it whole and entire. I, for my part, can well describe the movements of faith, but I cannot make them. When one would learn the swimming-movements, then can one let oneself be hung in straps from the ceiling; one describeth indeed the movements, but one swimmeth not; thus can I describe the movements of faith, but when I am cast into the water I do indeed swim (for I am no wader), but I make other movements, I make the movements of infinity, while faith doeth the opposite — after having made the movements of infinity, it maketh those of finitude. Blessed be he who can make these movements; he doeth the marvelous, and I shall never grow weary of admiring him, whether it be Abraham, or it be the slave in Abraham's house, whether it be a professor of philosophy or a poor serving-maid, is to me absolutely indifferent; I look only upon the movements. But upon them I do also look, and I let myself be cheated neither by myself nor by any man. The knights of the infinite resignation are easily known; their gait is hovering, bold. They, on the other hand, who bear the treasure of faith, easily disappoint, because their outward bearing hath a striking resemblance to that which both the infinite resignation and faith deeply despise — to philistinism. I confess sincerely, in my practice I have not found any reliable specimen, without my for that reason wishing to deny that perhaps every other man is such a specimen. Meanwhile I have for several years sought it in vain. Men generally travel the world round to behold rivers and mountains, new stars, motley-feathered birds, mis-shapen fishes, ridiculous human races; one giveth oneself up to that brutish stupor that gapeth at existence, and supposeth that one hath seen something. This occupieth me not. Did I, however, know where such a knight of faith dwelt, then would I journey to him on foot; for this marvel occupieth me absolutely. I would not let him out of my sight a moment; every minute would I watch how he bore himself in the movements; I would account myself provided for in life, and divide my time betwixt looking upon him and exercising myself, and so spend all my time in admiring him. As I said, I have found no such one; meanwhile I can well think him. Here he is. The acquaintance is made; I am presented to him. The instant I first set my eyes upon him, I cast him from me again that same moment, take a leap backward, clap my hands together, and say half aloud: “Lord God! is this the man, is it really he? — he looketh just like a tax-collector.” Notwithstanding it is he. I draw a little nearer, watch the smallest movement, whether there should not show itself a little uneven fractional telegraphing from the infinite, a glance, a look, a gesture, a melancholy, a smile, that betrayed the infinite in its incongruity with the finite. No! I examine his figure from top to toe, whether there should not be a chink through which the infinite peeped out. No! He is solid through and through. His footing? It is firm, belongeth wholly to finitude; no spruce burgher who walketh out of a Sunday afternoon to Frederiksberg treadeth more solidly upon the earth; he belongeth wholly to the world, no philistine could belong to it more. Nothing is to be discovered of that strange and lofty nature whereby one knoweth the knight of the infinite. He delighteth himself in everything, taketh part in everything, and every time one seeth him take part in the particular, it is with a persistence which marketh the earthly man whose soul cleaveth fast unto such things. He goeth about his work. When one looketh upon him, one would think he were a clerk who had lost his soul in Italian book-keeping, so punctual is he. He keepeth holiday on Sunday. He goeth to church. No heavenly look, nor any sign of the incommensurable, betrayeth him; if one knew him not, it were impossible to single him out from the rest of the throng; for his sound, vigorous psalm-singing proveth at most that he hath a good chest. Of an afternoon he goeth to the wood. He rejoiceth over all that he seeth, over the throng of people, the new omnibuses, the Sound — when one meeteth him on the Strandvei, one would think he were some shopkeeper let loose; just so doth he enjoy himself; for he is no poet, and I have in vain sought to entice from him the poetic incommensurability. Toward evening he goeth home; his gait is unwearied as a postman's. On the way he thinketh that his wife hath surely some special little warm dish for him,

when he cometh home, e.g. a roast lamb's head with greens. If he met one of like mind, he could go on talking with him all the way to Østerport about that dish, with a passion that would befit a restaurateur. By chance he hath not four shillings, and yet he believeth fully and firmly that his wife hath that dainty dish for him. Hath she it, then it shall be an enviable sight for fine folk, an inspiriting sight for the common man, to see him eat; for his appetite is stronger than Esau's. His wife hath it not — strangely enough, he is altogether the same. On the way he passeth a building-place; he meeteth another man. They speak together a moment; in a flash he raiseth a building, he disposeth of all the means thereto. The stranger leaveth him with the thought, surely that was a capitalist; while my admired knight thinketh: yes, did it come to that, I could easily get it. He lieth in an open window and watcheth the square in which he dwelleth; everything that passeth, that a rat slippeth down under a gutter-board, that the children play, all occupieth him with a calm in existence as though he were a girl of sixteen. And yet he is no genius; for the incommensurability of genius I have in vain sought to spy out in him. — He smoketh his pipe of an evening; when one looketh upon him, one would swear it was the bacon-monger across the way, who vegetateth in the twilight. He letteth things go with a carelessness as though he were a frivolous good-for-nothing, and yet every moment he liveth, he buyeth the seasonable time at the dearest price; for he doeth not so much as the least thing without it being by virtue of the absurd. And yet, yet — yea, I could become furious thereat, if for no other cause than envy — yet hath this man done, and doeth at every moment, the movement of infinity. He draineth in the infinite resignation the deep melancholy of existence; he knoweth the blessedness of infinity; he hath felt

the pain of forsaking everything, the dearest a man hath in the world; and yet finitude tasteth as sweet to him as to him who never knew anything higher; for his abiding in finitude hath no trace of a cowed and frightened drilling, and yet he hath this assurance to delight in it, as though it were the surest of all. And yet, yet, the whole earthly figure he bringeth forth is a new creation by virtue of the absurd. He resigned all things infinitely, and then grasped all things again by virtue of the absurd. He maketh constantly the movement of infinity, but he maketh it with such correctness and certainty that he constantly bringeth out finitude, and there is not a second wherein one suspecteth aught else. It is said to be the most difficult task for a dancer to leap into a determinate position, in such wise that there be no second wherein he is grasping for the position, but in the leap itself standeth in the position. Perhaps no dancer can do it — this doth that knight. The mass of men live forlorn in worldly sorrow and gladness; these are the wallflowers, who come not into the dance. The knights of infinity are dancers and have elevation. They make the movement upward and fall down again, and this also is no unblessed pastime, and not unlovely to look upon. But every time they fall down, they cannot at once take the position; they totter for a moment, and this tottering showeth that, after all, they are strangers in the world. It is more or less striking, according as they have art; but even the most artful of these knights cannot conceal this tottering. One needeth not see them in the air, one needeth only to see them in the moment they touch and have touched the earth — and one knoweth them. But to be able so to fall down that in the same second it looketh as if one stood and walked, to transmute the leap of life into a walk, absolutely to express the sublime in the pedestrian — that can only that knight do, — and this is the one and only marvel.

Yet this marvel may so easily deceive, that I will therefore describe the movements in a definite case, that may illuminate their relation to actuality; for it is upon this that everything turneth. A young swain falleth in love with a princess, and the entire content of his life lieth in this love; and yet the relation is such that it impossibly admitteth of being realized, impossibly admitteth of being translated from ideality into reality *. The slaves of wretchedness, the frogs in the swamp of life, will of course croak: such a love is folly, and the rich brewer's widow is a fully as good and solid a match. Let them undisturbed go on quacking in the swamp. The knight of the infinite resignation doeth not so; he giveth not up his love, not for all the glory of the world. He is no fool. He first satisfieth himself that it really is unto him the content of life, and his soul is too sound and too proud to lavish the smallest thing upon a debauch. He is not cowardly; he feareth not to let it steal into his most secret, his most retired thoughts, to let it twine itself in countless coils about every ligament of his consciousness — should the love prove unhappy, he will never be able to tear himself out of it. He feeleth a blessed voluptuousness in letting love thrill through every nerve of him, and yet his soul is solemn as that of him who hath drained the cup of poison and feeleth how the juice penetrateth every drop of blood — for this mo- *) It followeth of itself, that any other interest whatsoever, in which an individual hath the entire reality of actuality concentrated for himself, can, when it sheweth itself unrealizable, occasion the movement of resignation. I have, however, chosen a love affair to display the movements upon, because this interest will be the more easily understood, and so dispenseth me from all preliminary considerations, which in a deeper sense can occupy only the very few.

ment is life and death. When he hath thus drawn the whole of love into himself and become absorbed therein, then he lacketh not courage to attempt and to venture all. He surveyeth the relations of life; he calleth together the swift thoughts which, like trained pigeons, obey his every nod; he swingeth his staff over them, and they hurl themselves in every direction. But when they all return, all of them as messengers of sorrow, and explain to him that it is an impossibility, then he becometh still; he dismisseth them; he is alone, and then he undertaketh the movement. If what I here say is to have any meaning, then it must be that the movement is made normally *. The knight will then, first of all, have the strength to concentrate the entire content of life and the meaning of actuality into one single wish. Lacketh a man this concentration, this closure — is his soul from the beginning dispersed in the manifold — then cometh he never to make the movement; he will in life act shrewdly as those money-men who place their capital in many different securities, in order to win on the one when they lose on the other — in short, ein seliger Sprung in die Ewigkeit.

so is he no knight. Next, the knight will have the strength to concentrate the entire result of the operation of thought into one single act of consciousness. Lacketh he this closure, is his soul from the beginning dispersed in the manifold, then will he never have time to make the movement; he will be ever running errands in life, never entering into eternity; for even in the moment he is nearest thereto, he will suddenly discover that he hath forgotten somewhat, for which he must turn back. In the next moment, will he think, it is possible, and that is also quite true; but by such considerations one cometh never to make the movement, but by their aid one sinketh deeper and deeper into the mire.

The knight, then, maketh the movement, but which? Will he forget the whole? — for therein also lieth, indeed, a kind of concentration. No! For the knight contradicteth not himself, and it is a contradiction to forget the whole content of one's life and yet remain the same. To become another, he feeleth no impulse, and by no means accounteth it the great thing. Only the lower natures forget themselves and become something new. Thus hath the butterfly altogether forgotten that it was a caterpillar, perhaps it can in turn so utterly forget that it was a butterfly, that it can become a fish. The deeper natures never forget themselves and never become anything other than what they were. The knight will, then, remember all; but this remembering is precisely the pain, and yet he is in the infinite resignation reconciled with existence. The love for that princess became unto him the expression of an eternal love, took on a religious character, transfigured itself into a love for the eternal Being, who, though He denied the fulfilment, yet in turn reconciled him in the eternal consciousness of its validity in a form of eternity, which no actuality can take from him. Fools and young people prate that all things are possible to a man. It is, however, a great error. Spiritually speaking, all things are possible; but in the world of finitude there is much that is not possible. This impossible the knight, however, maketh possible thereby, that he expresseth it spiritually; but spiritually he expresseth it thereby, that he renounceth it. The wish, that would have led him out into actuality, but stranded upon impossibility, is now bent inward, but it is therefore not lost, neither forgotten. Now it is the obscure stirrings of the wish in him that awaken the remembrance, now he awakeneth it himself; for he is too proud to be willing that what was the entire content of his life should have been the matter of a fleeting moment. He keepeth this love young, and it increaseth with him in years and in beauty. On the other hand, he hath need of no occasion of finitude for its growth. From the moment he hath made the movement, the princess is lost. He hath no need of these erotic thrillings of the nerve at the sight of the beloved, &c.; neither hath he need, in a finite sense, constantly to take leave of her, because in an eternal sense he remembereth her, and he knoweth full well that those lovers who are so eager once again to see one another for a last farewell, are right to be eager, right to suppose that it is the last time, for they soonest forget one another. He hath grasped the deep secret, that even in loving another man one ought to be enough unto oneself. He taketh no finite account any longer of what the princess doeth, and precisely this proveth that he hath made the movement infinitely. Here may one have occasion to see whether the movement in the individual is true or feigned. There was the man who also believed that he had made the movement; but lo, time passed, the princess did somewhat else, she married, for example, a prince — then his soul lost the elasticity of resignation. He showed thereby that he had not made the movement rightly; for he who hath resigned infinitely, he is enough unto himself. The knight annulleth not his resignation; he keepeth his love just as young as it was in the first moment, he never letteth it slip from him, precisely because he hath made the movement infinitely. What the princess doeth cannot disturb him; it is only the lower natures who have the law of their actions in another man, the premises of their actions outside themselves. Is the princess, on the contrary, of like mind, then will the beautiful thing come forth. She will then introduce herself into that order of knighthood, into which one is not admitted by ballot, but of which every one is a member who hath the courage to introduce himself, the order of knighthood which thereby proveth its immortality, that it maketh no distinction between man and woman. She, too, will keep her love young and sound; she, too, will have overcome her woe, even though she lieth not, as it standeth in the ballad, every night by her lord's side. These twain will then through all eternity suit one another, with such a measured harmonia praestabilita, that, if ever the moment came, a moment that doth not, however, finitely occupy them, for then they grow old, if ever the moment came that allowed them to give to love its expression in time, then would they be in a position to begin precisely where they would have begun, had they originally been united. He who understandeth this, whether he be a man or a woman, can never be deceived; for it is only the lower natures that imagine themselves deceived. No maiden, who is not so proud, properly understandeth how to love; but is she so proud, then can all the cunning and craft of the world not deceive her.

In the infinite resignation there is peace and rest; every man who will it, who hath not abased himself by — what is yet more dreadful than to be too proud — making light of himself, can chasten himself to make this movement, which in its pain reconcileth with existence. The infinite resignation is that shirt whereof a tale is told in an old folk-legend. The thread is spun under tears, bleached by tears, the shirt sewn in tears; but then it also protecteth better than iron and steel. The imperfection of the folk-legend is, that a third party can fashion this linen. The secret of life is that every one must sew it for himself, and the remarkable thing is that a man can sew it just as well as a woman. In the infinite resignation there is peace and rest and consolation in the pain — that is, when the movement is made normally. It would not, however, be hard for me to write a whole book, were I to go through the various misunderstandings, the wrong-headed positions, the slovenly movements, I have come upon merely in my little practice. Men believe very little upon spirit, and yet it is precisely a question of spirit to make this movement; it is a question that it be not a one-sided result of a dira necessitas, and the more this is present, the more questionable it becometh always whether the movement is normal. So when men would suppose that the cold, barren necessity necessarily must be present, then they say therewith that no man can experience death before he really dieth, which appeareth to me a crass materialism. Yet in our age men concern themselves less with making clean movements. Did one, who had to learn to dance, say: now for centuries one generation after another hath learned positions, it is high time that I draw advantage to myself therefrom, and without further ado begin upon the française — then men would surely laugh a little at him; but in the world of the spirit men find it exceedingly plausible. What, then, is culture? I supposed it was the curriculum which the individual ran through in order to overtake himself; and he who will not pass through this curriculum, him it helpeth very little to have been born in the most enlightened age.

The infinite resignation is the last stage which goeth before faith, in such wise that whosoever hath not made this movement hath not faith; for it is first in the infinite resignation that I become clear to myself in my eternal validity, and first then can there be question of laying hold of existence by virtue of faith.

We will now let the knight of faith appear in the case spoken of. He doeth altogether the same as the other knight: he giveth up infinitely the love which is the content of his life, he is reconciled in the pain — but then the marvel cometh, he maketh yet one more movement, more wondrous than all the rest; for he saith: I yet believe that I shall get her, namely by virtue of the absurd, by virtue of the fact that for God all things are possible. The absurd belongeth not to those differences which lie within the proper compass of the understanding. It is not identical with the improbable, the unexpected, the unlooked-for. In the moment the knight resigned, he had assured himself of the impossibility, humanly speaking; this was the result of the understanding, and he had energy enough to think it. In an infinite sense it was, on the other hand, possible — that is, by resigning thereon; but this possessing is at the same time also a giving up, and yet this possessing is for the understanding no absurdity; for the understanding kept on being right, that in the world of wretchedness, where it ruleth, it was and remained an impossibility. This consciousness the knight of faith hath as clearly; the only thing, therefore, that can save him is the absurd, and this he layeth hold of by faith. He acknowledgeth, then, the impossibility, and in the same moment he believeth the absurd; for would he, without with all his soul's passion and his whole heart acknowledging the impossibility, persuade himself that he hath the faith, then he deceiveth himself, and his testimony hath nowhere a home, since he hath not even come to the infinite resignation.

Faith is therefore no aesthetic stirring, but somewhat far higher, precisely because it hath resignation before it; it is not the heart's immediate impulse, but the paradox of existence. Thus, when a young maiden, in spite of all difficulties, holdeth herself yet assured that her wish shall surely be fulfilled, this assurance is by no means that of faith, and that notwithstanding she be brought up by Christian parents, and have, perhaps, gone for a whole year to the priest. She is assured in all her childlike naïveté and innocence; this assurance, too, ennobleth her being, and giveth her a supernatural stature, so that, like a thaumaturge, she can adjure the finite powers of existence, and make stones themselves to weep, while, on the other hand, she can in her flurry just as well run to Herod as to Pilate, and move the whole world with her prayers. Her assurance is right lovely, and one can learn much from her; but one thing one learneth not from her, one learneth not to make movements; for her assurance dareth not, in resignation's pain, look impossibility in the face.

I can well perceive, then, that strength and energy and freedom of spirit are needed to make the infinite movement of resignation; I can also perceive that it can be done. The next thing astoundeth me, my brain reeleth in my head; for, having made the movement of resignation, now by virtue of the absurd to receive everything, to receive the wish, whole, unabridged — this is beyond human powers, this is a marvel. But this I can perceive, that the young maiden's assurance is only thoughtlessness in comparison with the immovableness of faith, although it hath perceived the impossibility. Every time I would make this movement, all groweth dark before mine eye; in the same instant I admire it absolutely, and in the same instant a prodigious anguish seizeth my soul, for what then is it to tempt God? And yet this movement is faith's, and remaineth so, even though philosophy, in order to confuse the concepts, would persuade us that it hath the faith, even though theology would sell it out at a bargain.

To resign there belongeth no faith, for that which I in resignation win is my eternal consciousness, and this is a purely philosophical movement, which I trust myself to make when it is required, and which I can chasten myself to make; for every time some finitude would grow over my head, then do I starve myself out, until I make the movement; for my eternal consciousness is my love to God, and this is to me higher than all. To resign there belongeth no faith, but to receive the very least more than my eternal consciousness there belongeth faith, for this is the paradoxical. Men often confound the movements. They say one needeth faith in order to give up everything; yea, one heareth it yet more strangely, that a man complaineth that he hath lost the faith, and when one looketh on the scale to see where he is, one seeth, strangely enough, that he hath only come to the point at which he is to make the infinite movement of resignation.
