If, however, it were something deeper that stirred in these twain, if there were earnestness to see the task, earnestness to begin, then will somewhat doubtless come of them; but ethics cannot help them — it is offended; for they have a secret from it, a secret which they have taken upon their own account and answer.
Aesthetics, then, demanded hiddenness and rewarded it; ethics demanded disclosure and punished hiddenness.

At times, however, aesthetics itself demandeth disclosure. When the hero, ensnared in the aesthetic illusion, thinketh by his silence to save another person, then doth it demand silence and reward it. When, on the contrary, the hero by his deed intervenest disturbingly in another person's life, then it demandeth disclosure. Here I stand at the tragic hero. I will for a moment consider Euripides's Iphigenia in Aulis. Agamemnon is to sacrifice Iphigenia. Aesthetics now demandeth silence of Agamemnon, insofar as it would be unworthy of the hero to seek consolation from any other person, just as he, out of consideration for the women, ought to hide it from them as long as possible. On the other hand, the hero, precisely in order to be a hero, must also be tested in the dreadful spiritual trial which the tears of Clytemnestra and Iphigenia will prepare for him. What doth aesthetics do? It hath a way out, it hath an old servant in readiness, who revealeth all to Clytemnestra. Now is everything in order.

Ethics, however, hath no accident and no old servant at hand. The aesthetic idea contradicteth itself as soon as it is to be carried out in actuality. Ethics therefore demandeth disclosure. The tragic hero showeth precisely his ethical courage in this, that, not ensnared in any aesthetic illusion, he is himself the one who proclaimeth to Iphigenia her fate. If he do this, then is the tragic hero the beloved son of ethics, in whom she hath good pleasure. If he be silent, it may be because he thereby believeth he maketh it easier for others, but it may also be because he thereby maketh it easier for himself. Yet this he knoweth himself to be free of. If he be silent, then doth he as the single individual take upon himself a responsibility, insofar as he overlooketh an argument that may come from without. This he as a tragic hero cannot do; for it is precisely on this account that ethics loveth him, that he constantly expresseth the universal. His heroic deed demandeth courage, but to this courage belongeth also that he doth not withdraw himself from any argumentation. Now it is certain that tears are a dreadful argumentum ad hominem, and there hath surely been one whom nothing could move, whom yet tears moved. In the play, Iphigenia getteth leave to weep; in actuality there should be granted her, as to Jephthah's daughter, two months in which to weep, not in solitude, but at her father's feet, and to use all her art, “which is only tears,” and to wind herself, “in stead of an olive branch,” about his knees (cf. v. 1224).
Aesthetics demanded disclosure, but helped itself with an accident; ethics demanded disclosure, and found in the tragic hero its satisfaction.

Notwithstanding the strictness with which ethics demandeth disclosure, it cannot be denied that secrecy and silence verily make a man great, precisely because they are determinations of inwardness. When Amor leaveth Psyche, he saith unto her: thou shalt bear a child who shall be a divine child if thou keep silence, but a human one if thou betray the secret. The tragic hero, who is ethics's favorite, is the pure human being; him I can also understand, and all his enterprise is also in the manifest. If I go further, then I constantly run up against the paradox, the divine and the demoniac; for silence is both. Silence is the demon's snare, and the more one is silent, the more dreadful the demon becometh; but silence is also the deity's communion with the single individual.

Before, however, I pass over to the story of Abraham, I will call forth a couple of poetic individualities. By the power of dialectics I keep them upon the peak, and as I swing the discipline of despair over them, I shall surely keep them from standing still,

that, if it be possible, in their anxiety they may discover one thing or another. Aristotle relateth in his Politics a story of a political disturbance in Delphi which had its ground in a marriage affair. The bridegroom, to whom the augurs predict a misfortune that shall have its origin in his marriage, suddenly altereth his plan in the decisive moment, when he cometh to fetch the bride — he will not hold the wedding. More I need not. In Delphi this

These movements and postures may indeed still become the object of aesthetic treatment; how far, on the contrary, faith and the whole life of faith may become so, I leave here undecided. Only will I, because it is always a joy to me to thank him to whom I owe somewhat, thank Lessing for the few hints concerning a Christian drama which are to be found in his Hamburgische Dramaturgie. He hath, however, fixed his gaze upon the purely divine side of this life (the consummated victory), and therefore hath he despaired; perhaps he would have judged otherwise had he given more heed to the purely human side. (Theologia viatorum.) What he saith is unmistakably very brief, in part evasive; but since I am always exceeding glad whensoever I can have occasion to bring Lessing in, I bring him in straightway. Lessing was not only one of the most comprehensive heads Germany hath owned; he was not only in possession of a quite rare promptness in his knowledge, which maketh that one may securely rely upon him and his autopsy without fearing to be deceived by loose citations that have nowhere a home, half-understood phrases drawn from unreliable handbooks, or to be disoriented by some stupid trumpeting forth of novelties which the elder writers had set forth far better — but he had besides a most uncommon gift for explaining what he himself had understood. There he stopped; in our age men go further, and explain more than they themselves have understood.

The historical catastrophe was, according to Aristotle, the following: in order to revenge themselves, the family slip a temple-vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple-robber. Event scarce went off without tears; were a poet to adopt it, he might surely count upon sympathy. Is it not dreadful that love, which often enough hath been an exile in life, is now also robbed of heaven's assistance? Is not the old saying that marriage is established in heaven here put to shame? Otherwise it is all the troubles and difficulties of finitude that, like evil spirits, would sunder the lovers, while love hath heaven on its side, and therefore this holy alliance vanquisheth all foes. Here it is heaven itself which sundereth what heaven itself hath, after all, joined together. Who would also have suspected this? least of all, surely, the young bride. Only a moment ago she sat in her chamber in all her beauty, and the lovely girls had conscientiously decked her out, so that they could answer for it before all the world, so that they had not only joy thereof but envy — yea, joy that it was impossible for them to be more envious, because it was impossible for her to be more beautiful. She sat alone in her chamber, and was transformed from beauty to beauty; for all that womanly art could achieve was used worthily to deck the worthy; but there was still wanting somewhat which the young girls had not dreamed of: a veil, finer, lighter, and yet more concealing than that in which the young girls had wrapped her — a bridal robe of which no young girl knew, or could be of help to her in. This, however, is a matter of indifference; for the question is not whether the family is shrewd or stupid in taking revenge — the family acquireth only ideal significance insofar as it is drawn into the hero's dialectic. It is, moreover, fateful enough that he, in seeking to flee the danger by not marrying, plungeth into it, and that his life in a twofold manner cometh into contact with the divine, first by the augur's saying, next by being condemned as a temple-robber.

It was an invisible, friendly power that hath its delight in adorning a bride, that wrapped her in it, without her knowing aught thereof; for she only saw how the bridegroom passed by and went up to the temple. She saw the door close behind him, and she became the more calm and blessed; for she knew that he now belonged to her more than ever. The temple's door opened, he stepped forth, but she lowered her eye in maidenly fashion, and therefore she saw not that his countenance was confused; but he saw that heaven was indeed envious of the bride's loveliness and of his happiness. The temple's door opened, the young girls saw the bridegroom step forth; but they saw not that his countenance was confused, for they were busy fetching the bride. Then she stepped forth in all her maidenly humility, and yet as a sovereign, surrounded by her train of young girls who curtsied before her, as the young girl ever curtsieth before a bride. So she stood at the head of the lovely company, and waited — it was but a moment, for the temple was right at hand — and the bridegroom came — but he passed by her door.

But I break off here; I am no poet, and proceed only dialectically. The first thing to be noted is that it is in the decisive moment that the hero receiveth that disclosure; he is then pure and without remorse, hath not lightly bound himself to the beloved. Next, he hath a divine pronouncement for him, or rather against him; he is then not, like those slender lovers and beloveds, governed by self-cleverness. It followeth furthermore of itself that this pronouncement maketh him just as unhappy as the bride — yea, a little more, since he is, after all, the occasion. For although it is true that the augurs predicted only a misfortune for him, the question is whether this misfortune be not of such a kind that, in striking him, it will likewise strike their wedded happiness. What shall he now do? 1) Shall he be silent and hold the wedding, and think: misfortune cometh perhaps not at once; in any event I have asserted my love and have not feared to make myself unhappy; but be silent I must, for else even the brief moment is forfeit. This seemeth plausible, but it is by no means so; for in that case he hath wronged the girl. He hath by his silence in a manner made the girl guilty; for had she known of it, she surely would never have given her consent to such a union. He shall then in the time of need have not only the misfortune to bear, but also the responsibility that he was silent, her righteous wrath that he was silent. 2) Shall he be silent and forbear to hold the wedding? In that case he must enter upon a mystification whereby he annihilateth himself in his relation to her. This perhaps aesthetics would approve. The catastrophe might then be shaped in likeness to the actual one, only that in the last moment it would come to an explanation, which, however, would be after the fact, since aesthetically considered it becometh a necessity to let him die — unless this science should see itself able to lift that ill-omened prophecy. In the meantime this conduct, however magnanimous it be, containeth a wrong against the girl and the actuality of her love. 3) Shall he speak? But to what end now this sketch, since I get no further than to the tragic hero? Because it was, after all, possible that it might cast a light upon the paradox. Everything dependeth, then, on what relation he standeth in to the augurs' pronouncement, which in one way or another becometh decisive for his life. Is this pronouncement publici juris, or is it a privatissimum? The scene is in Greece; an augur's pronouncement is intelligible to all — I mean not only that the single individual can lexically understand its content, but that the single individual can understand that an augur proclaimeth to the single individual the decision of heaven. The augur's pronouncement is then intelligible not only to the hero, but to all, and there resulteth no private relation to the deity therefrom. He may do what he will; what hath been foretold will come to pass, and he cometh neither by doing nor by leaving undone into a closer relation to the deity, becometh neither the object of its grace nor of its wrath. The outcome will every single individual be able to understand just as well as the hero, and there is no secret writing which is legible only to the hero. Insofar, then, as he would speak, he can do so admirably, for he can make himself understandable; insofar as he would be silent, it is because, by virtue of being the single individual, he would be higher than the universal, would dazzle himself with all manner of fantastic notions of how she will soon forget the matter, and so on.

If, on the contrary, heaven's will had not been proclaimed unto him by an augur, if it had come to his knowledge altogether privately, if it had set itself in an entirely private relation to him, then are we at the paradox, if otherwise it be (for my consideration is dilemmatic); for then could he not speak, however gladly he would. He enjoyed not himself in the silence, but he suffered the pain; yet this very pain was for him the assurance that he was justified. His silence had then its ground not in his wishing as the single individual to set himself in an absolute relation to the universal, but in his being as the single individual placed in an absolute relation to the absolute. He would also be able to find rest therein, according as I can imagine, while his magnanimous silence would constantly be disquieted by the demands of the ethical. It were generally to be wished that aesthetics would one day try to begin where, for so many years, it hath ended — namely, with the illusory magnanimity. So soon as it did this, it would work directly into the hands of the religious; for this power is the only one which can save the aesthetic out of its struggle with the ethical. Queen Elizabeth sacrificed unto the State her love for Essex by signing his death warrant. This was a heroic deed, even though there was a little personal offense in the play, that he had not sent her the ring. As is well known, he had done so, but by the malice of a lady-in-waiting it had been kept back. Elizabeth received, so it is told ni fallor, the news thereof; thereupon she sat for ten days with one finger in her mouth, biting it without speaking a single word, and then she died. This was a task for a poet who knew how to wrest her mouth open; otherwise it is at most usable for a ballet master, with whom the poet in our age often enough confoundeth himself.

Now will I let a sketch follow in the direction of the demoniac. For this I can use the legend of Agnete and the Merman. The Merman is a seducer who shooteth up out of the abyss's hiding-place, and in wild lust seizeth and breaketh the innocent flower that, in all its grace, stood at the seashore and pensively bowed its head at the murmuring of the sea. This hath hitherto been the poets' meaning. Let us make a change. The Merman was a seducer. He hath called upon Agnete, by his ingratiating speech he hath lured forth the hidden in her, she hath found in the Merman what she sought, after which she stared down at the bottom of the sea. Agnete will follow him. The Merman hath set her upon his arm, Agnete twineth herself about his neck; she giveth herself trustingly with her whole soul to the stronger one; he standeth already at the seashore, he leaneth out over the sea to plunge down with his prey — then Agnete looketh upon him yet once more, not fearfully, not doubting, not proud of her happiness, not intoxicated in lust, but absolutely believing, but absolutely humble as the lowly flower she deemed herself to be, absolutely trustingly she committeth to him with this glance her whole fate. — And lo! the sea roareth no more, its wild voice falleth silent, the passion of nature, which is the Merman's strength, leaveth him in the lurch, it becometh a dead calm — and still doth Agnete look upon him in that wise. Then sinketh the Merman together, he cannot withstand the power of innocence, his element becometh faithless to him, he cannot seduce Agnete. He leadeth her home again, he explaineth to her that he only would show her how beautiful the sea is when it is still, and Agnete believeth him. — Then he turneth back alone, and the sea storms; but the despair in the Merman storms more wildly. He can seduce Agnete, he can seduce a hundred Agnetes, he can charm any girl — but Agnete hath conquered, and the Merman hath lost her. Only as prey can she become his; faithfully he can belong to no girl, for he is, after all, but a Merman. I have allowed myself a small alteration with the Merman; in essentials I have also altered Agnete a little; for in the legend Agnete is not altogether without guilt, just as it is, generally, nonsense and dalliance and an offense against the female sex to imagine a seduction wherein the girl hath no, no, no guilt at all. Agnete is in the legend, that I may modernize my expression a little, a woman who demandeth the interesting, and any such can always be sure that there is a Merman

We will now give the merman a human consciousness, and let his being a merman betoken a human pre-existence, in whose consequence his life was entangled. There is naught to hinder him from becoming a hero; for the step which he now taketh is reconciling. He is saved by Agnes; the seducer is crushed; he hath bowed beneath the power of innocence; never more can he seduce. But in the same instant two powers contend over him: repentance, and Agnes and repentance. If repentance taketh him alone, then is he hidden; if Agnes and repentance take him, then is he manifest.

Insofar now as repentance lays hold upon the merman and he remaineth hidden, then hath he indeed made Agnes unhappy; for Agnes loved him in all her innocence: she believed it was true that, in that moment when he appeared even to her changed, however well he hid it, he only wished to show her the beautiful stillness of the sea. The merman himself, however, in respect of passion, becometh yet more unhappy; for he loved Agnes with a manifoldness of passions, and besides hath a new guilt to bear. The demonic in repentance will now indeed explain to him that this is precisely his punishment, and the more it tortureth him, the better.

If he giveth himself up to this demonic, then doth he perhaps make yet another attempt to save Agnes — in such wise as one can, in a certain sense, save a man by means of evil. He knoweth that Agnes loveth him. Could he wrest from Agnes this love, then is she in a manner saved. But how? To reckon upon this, that an open-hearted confession should awaken her loathing — for that the merman is too clever. He may then perhaps see fit to inflame all dark passions in her, to taunt her, to mock her, to make her love a laughing-stock, if possible to provoke her pride. He will spare himself no torment; for this is the deep contradiction in the demonic, and there dwelleth in a certain sense infinitely more good in a demonic person than in trivial men. The more selfish Agnes is, the more easily will she be deceived (for it is only very inexperienced folk who think it easy to deceive innocence; existence is most profound, and it is the easiest thing for the wise to dupe the wise) — but the more dreadful will the merman's sufferings be. The more cunningly his deceit is laid, the less will Agnes bashfully hide her suffering from him; she will use every means, which then will not be without effect — that is to say, not to shake him, but to torture him.

By means of the demonic the merman would, then, be the single individual who as the single individual was higher than the universal. The demonic hath the same property as the divine: that the single individual can enter into an absolute relation thereto. This is the analogy, the counterpart, to that paradox of which we speak. It hath therefore a certain similarity, which can deceive. Thus the merman hath, to all appearance, this proof that his silence is justified — that in it he suffereth all his pain. There is, meanwhile, no doubt that he can speak. A tragic hero he can become, in my view a grandiose tragic hero, if he speaketh. Few perhaps will so much as grasp wherein the grandiose lieth*. Aesthetics doth at times treat something similar with its wonted dalliance. The merman is saved by Agnes, and the whole endeth in a happy marriage. A happy marriage! that is easy enough. — courage to wrest from himself every self-deception that he could make Agnes happy by his art; he will have courage, humanly speaking, to crush Agnes. For the rest, I will here only make a psychological remark. The more selfishly Agnes hath been developed, the more dazzling will the self-deception be; nay, it is not unthinkable that it could come to pass in actuality that a merman, by his demonic shrewdness, humanly speaking, not only had saved an Agnes, but had brought something extraordinary out of an Agnes; for a demon knoweth how to torture forces out of the very weakest person, and he can in his own way mean very well by a man. The merman standeth upon a dialectical peak. If he be saved out of the demonic in repentance, then are there two ways possible. He can hold himself back, remain in the hidden, but not rely upon his shrewdness. He cometh then, as the single individual, not into an absolute relation to the demonic, but findeth rest in the counter-paradox that the deity will save Agnes. (Thus surely would the Middle Ages make the movement; for the merman is, evidently, according to its conception, made over to the cloister.) Or he can be saved by Agnes. This must now not be understood as if by Agnes's love he should be saved from becoming, in time to come, a seducer (this is an aesthetic attempt at rescue, which always passeth by the main thing — namely, the continuity of the merman's life); for in this respect he is saved; he is saved insofar as he becometh manifest. He then weddeth Agnes. In the meantime he must take refuge in the paradox. For when the single individual hath, by his guilt, come outside the universal, then can he return thereto only by virtue of being, as the single individual, in an absolute relation to the absolute. Here will I now make a remark by which I say more than hath been said at any point in the foregoing**. Sin is not the first immediacy; sin is a later immediacy. In sin the single individual is already, in the direction of the demonic paradox, higher than the universal, because it is a contradiction of the universal to demand itself of him who lacketh the conditio sine qua non. If philosophy, among other things, also gave thought to this, that it might occur to a man to wish to act according to its teaching, one would get a strange comedy out of it. An ethic that ignoreth sin is an utterly idle science; but if it maketh sin valid, then is it eo ipso beyond itself. Philosophy teacheth that the immediate is to be annulled. This is true enough; but what is not true is that sin is, without further ado, the immediate, just as little as faith, without further ado, is the immediate. — A happy marriage! That is easy enough. If, on the other hand, ethics is to give the address at the wedding, then I think it will be another matter. Aesthetics throweth the cloak of love over the merman, and so all is forgotten. It is also careless enough to think that it goeth with a marriage as at an auction, where everything is sold in the condition in which it is found at the hammer-blow. It only seeth to it that the lovers obtain each other; the rest it troubleth itself not about. Could it but see what cometh to pass thereafter; but for that it hath no time, it is straightway at full pitch in clapping a new loving pair together. Aesthetics is the most faithless of all the sciences. Whoever hath truly loved it becometh, in a certain sense, unhappy; but whoever hath never loved it is and remaineth a wretch. — In such manner, as if by Agnes's love he should be saved from in future becoming a seducer (this is an aesthetic attempt at rescue, which always passeth by the main thing, namely the continuity of the merman's life); for in this respect he is saved; he is saved insofar as he becometh manifest. He then weddeth Agnes. Yet must he take refuge in the paradox. For when the single individual hath by his guilt come outside the universal, he can only return to it by virtue of being, as the single individual, in an absolute relation to the absolute.

The merman's movements I can therefore understand, while I cannot understand Abraham; for the merman cometh precisely through the paradox to wish to realize the universal. For if he remain hidden and consecrate himself to all the torments of repentance, then becometh he a demon, and as such is annihilated. If he remain hidden, but mean not shrewdly that by being himself tortured in the bondage of repentance he can work Agnes loose, then doth he obtain peace, but he is lost to this world. If he become manifest, letting himself be saved by Agnes, then is he the greatest man I can imagine; for it is only aesthetics that lightly thinketh to praise the power of love by letting the lost one be loved by an innocent maiden and thereby saved; it is only aesthetics that seeth wrongly, and believeth that the maiden is the heroine, instead that the merman is. The merman cannot then belong to Agnes save that he, after having made the infinite movement of repentance, yet make one more movement, the movement by virtue of the absurd. By his own strength he can make the movement of repentance; but he useth also absolutely his whole strength thereto, and therefore he cannot possibly by his own strength come back again and grasp actuality. When one hath not passion enough either to make the one or the other movement, when one slouches through life, repenteth a little, and thinketh that the rest will go by itself, then hath one once and for all renounced living in the idea, and so one can very easily attain, and help others to attain, the highest — that is, to bedazzle oneself and others into the conception that in the world of spirit it goeth as in a game of gnav, where everything goeth on at random. One can then divert oneself by considering how strange it is, that precisely in an age when everyone, after all, can do the highest, doubt about the immortality of the soul can be so widespread; for he who hath truly made even the movement of infinity scarcely doubteth. The conclusions of passion are the only reliable ones — that is, the only convincing ones. Happily, existence here is more loving, more faithful, than what wise men assert; for it excludeth no man, not even the lowliest; it dupeth no one, for in the world of spirit only he is duped who dupeth himself. It is the opinion of all, and insofar as I dare allow myself to judge thereof, it is also my opinion, that it is not the highest to enter a cloister; but it is by no means therefore my opinion that in our age, when no man entereth a cloister, every one is greater than those deep and earnest souls who found rest in a cloister. How many in our age have passion enough to think it, and then to judge themselves honestly? The mere notion of so taking time upon one's conscience, of giving it time in its sleepless tirelessness to investigate every secret thought, in such wise that one, if one doth not at every moment make the movement by virtue of the noblest and holiest in a man, with anxiety and dread can discover*, and if by nothing else, then by anxiety lure forth that dim stirring which yet hideth itself in every human life, while, when one liveth in society with others, one so easily forgetteth, so easily letteth go of it, is held up in so many ways, getteth occasion to begin afresh —

This men do not believe in our serious age, and yet it is remarkable enough that even in heathendom, which by its essence is more frivolous and less thoroughly reflected, the two real representatives of the Greek view of existence — γνῶθι σεαυτόν — each in his own way have hinted that, by sinking into oneself, one first and foremost discovereth the disposition to evil. That I am thinking of Pythagoras and Socrates, I need surely not say.

this notion alone, grasped with seemly reverence, I thought might chastise many an individual in our age, who already imagineth that he hath come to the highest. Yet about this men in our age, who have come to the highest, concern themselves but little, while no age, like precisely this one, hath been forfeit to the comic. And it is incomprehensible that it hath not already come to pass that the age itself, by a generatio aequivoca, hath spawned its hero — the demon, who relentlessly will perform the dreadful play, to bring the whole age to laughter, and to make it forget that it laugheth at itself. Or what is existence worth more than to be laughed at, when one hath already in one's twentieth year come to the highest? And yet, what higher movement hath the age devised since that hour when men gave up entering the cloister? Is it not a wretched life-wisdom, cleverness, faintheartedness, that sitteth in the high seat, that cravenly persuadeth men that they have done the highest, and slyly holdeth them back from even attempting the lesser? He who hath made the cloister-movement hath only one movement remaining, that of the absurd. How many in our age understand what the absurd is? How many in our age live in such wise that they have given up everything, or have got everything? How many are even so honest that they know what they can and what they cannot? And is it not true that, insofar as one findeth such men, one findeth them most readily among the less educated, and in part among women? In a kind of clairvoyance the age revealeth, as a demonic always revealeth himself without understanding himself, its defect; for it demandeth again and again the comic. Should this really be that which the age needeth? Should the theatre perhaps need a new piece in which it should be made ridiculous that one died of love? Or would it not rather be saving for the age, if it came to pass amongst us, if the age became witness to such an event, that it might at last get courage to believe in the power of spirit, courage not cowardly to stifle the better in itself, enviously to stifle it in others — by laughter? Should the age really need a ridiculous Erscheinung of one awakened, in order to get something to laugh at; or should it not rather need that such an inspired figure remind it of what was forgotten?

Wert thou disposed to have a sketch in similar style, which yet, because the passion of repentance was not set in motion, would become more touching, then for this one might use a story which occurreth in the Book of Tobit. The young Tobias would wed Sarah, the daughter of Raguel and Edna. With this maiden it standeth in a sad case. She hath been given to seven men, all of whom have perished in the bridal chamber. This is, in the direction of my sketch, a blemish in the story; for the comic effect is well-nigh inevitable, when the thought is awakened of a maiden's seven fruitless attempts to be married, although she came quite near thereto, as near as a student who hath gone seven times rejected to the Attestats. In the Book of Tobit the accent lieth elsewhere, and therefore is the high number of importance, and in a certain sense even tragically contributing; for so much the greater is the young Tobias's high-mindedness, partly insofar as he is his parents' only son (6, 15), partly because the deterrent presseth itself the more upon him. This must therefore be put aside. Sarah is then a maiden who hath never loved, who still keepeth a young maiden's blessedness, her enormous priority bond on existence, her „Vollmachtbrief zum Glücke“ — to love a man with her whole heart. And yet she is more unhappy than any; for she knoweth that the evil demon, who loveth her, will slay the bridegroom on the wedding-night. I have read of much sorrow, but I doubt whether anywhere there be found so deep a sorrow as that which lieth in this maiden's life. When misfortune cometh from without, there is yet consolation to be found. Even if existence brought a man not what could have made him happy, it is yet a consolation that he might have received it. But the unfathomable sorrow which no time can disperse, no time heal — to know that it would help nothing, even though existence did everything! A Greek author hideth in his simple naïveté so infinitely much, when he saith: πάντως γὰρ οὐδεὶς Ἔρωτα ἔφυγεν ἢ φεύξεται, μέχρις ἂν κάλλος ᾖ καὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ βλέπωσιν (cf. Longi Pastoralia). There hath been many a maiden who became unhappy in love; but she did become so. Sarah was so before she became so. It is heavy not to find the one to whom one can give oneself, but it is unspeakably heavy not to be able to give oneself. A young maiden giveth herself, and then it is said: now is she no longer free; but Sarah was never free, and yet she had never given herself. It is heavy if a maiden gave herself and was deceived; but Sarah was deceived before she gave herself. What sorrow of the world lieth not in what followeth, when Tobias at length will wed her! What wedding-ceremonies, what preparations! No maiden hath been deceived as Sarah was; for she was deceived of the most blessed of all things, the absolute riches which even the poorest maiden owneth — deceived of the secure, unbounded, unbridled, untrammelled abandon of self-giving; for there must first be smoke, when the heart of the fish and the liver were laid upon the glowing embers. And how must the mother not take leave of the daughter, who, deceived like herself of all things, must in continuity therewith deceive the mother of the most beautiful thing! One need but read the story. Edna prepared the chamber and led Sarah into it, and wept, and received her daughter's tears. And she said unto her: my child, be of good cheer! May the Lord of heaven and earth give thee joy for this thy sorrow! Daughter, be of good cheer. And now the wedding moment — let one read it, if one can for tears: but when they were both shut in together, Tobias rose up from the bed and said:
Stand up, sister! and let us pray that the Lord may have mercy upon us (8, 4).

If a poet read this story, if he would use it, I wager a hundred to one that he would lay everything upon the young Tobias. The heroism of being willing to risk his life in such manifest peril — whereof the story remindeth us yet again; for Raguel saith on the morning after the wedding to Edna: send one of the maidens, and let her see whether he liveth, but if not, that I may bury him, and no one shall know it (cf. 8, 13) — this heroism would become the task. I take the liberty of proposing another. It is bold and brave and chivalrous of Tobias to act so; but every man who hath not the courage thereto is a sissy who knoweth neither what love is, nor what it is to be a man, nor what is worth living for; he hath not even grasped the little mystery, that it is better to give than to receive, and hath no inkling of the great: that it is far harder to receive than to give — that is to say, when one hath had courage to do without and in the hour of need was not cowardly. Nay, Sarah she is heroine. Her will I draw nigh unto, as I have never drawn nigh to any maiden, nor felt myself tempted in thought to draw nigh to any I have read about. For what love of God belongeth not thereto, in order to be willing to let oneself be healed, when one is in this manner from the beginning unhinged through no fault of one's own — from the beginning a botched specimen of a human being! What ethical maturity to take upon oneself the responsibility of permitting the beloved such a daring venture! What humility before another person! What faith in God, that she should not in the next moment hate the man to whom she owed everything!
Let Sarah be a man, and the demonic lieth ready at hand. The proud, noble nature can endure all things, but one thing it cannot endure: it cannot endure

compassion. There lieth therein an outrage, which can only be inflicted upon him by a higher power; for by himself he can never become its object. If he hath sinned, he can bear the punishment without despairing; but to be without guilt singled out from his mother's womb as a victim of compassion, a sweet savour in its nostrils — this he cannot endure. Compassion hath a strange dialectic: in one moment it demandeth guilt, in the next it will not have it; and therefore being predestined to compassion becometh more and more dreadful, the more the individual's misfortune lieth in the direction of the spiritual. But Sarah hath no guilt, she is cast forth as prey to all sufferings, and on top of that must be tortured by men's compassion; for even I, who admire her more than Tobias loved her, even I cannot mention her name without saying: poor maiden. Let a man be in Sarah's place, let him know that, if he will love a maiden, then a hellish spirit cometh and murdereth the beloved on the wedding-night — then it is well possible that he chose the demonic; he shut himself up in himself, and said in the manner that a demonic nature speaketh in secret: “Thanks, I am no friend of ceremonies and elaborateness; I desire not at all the joy of love; I might as well become a Bluebeard, who hath his delight in seeing the maidens sink down on the wedding-night.” One generally getteth to know very little about the demonic, although this region precisely in our age hath a valid claim to be discovered, and although the observer, when he otherwise knoweth how to set himself in a little rapport with the demon, can almost use any man at least momentarily. Shakespeare is and remaineth ever in this direction a hero. Yon dreadful demon, the most demonic figure that Shakespeare hath portrayed, but also portrayed matchlessly: Gloster (afterwards Richard the Third) — what made him a demon? Plainly this, that he could not bear compassion, to which from childhood he had been given over. His monologue in the first act of Richard the Third is worth more than entire moral systems, which have no inkling of the terrors of existence or of the explanation.

Ich, roh geprägt, und aller Reize baar, / Vor leicht sich dreh'nden Nymphen mich zu brüsten; / Ich, so verkürzt um schönes Ebenmass, / Geschändet von der tückischen Natur, / Entstellt, verwahrlost, vor der Zeit gesandt / In diese Welt des Athmens, halb kaum fertig / Gemacht, und zwar so lahm und ungeziemend, / Dass Hunde bellen, hink' ich wo vorbei.

Such natures as Gloster's one cannot save by mediating them into an idea of community. Ethics in truth doth but mock at them, as it were a mockery of Sarah, did it say to her: why expressest thou not the universal and marriest? Such natures are from their ground in the paradox, and they are by no means more imperfect than other men, only that they are either lost in the demonic paradox or saved in the divine. Men have time and again taken pleasure in this, that witches, gnomes, trolls and the like were misshapen creatures; and it is undeniable that every man hath an inclination, when he seeth a misshapen person, at once to attach to it the conception of a moral depravity. What a monstrous injustice; for the relation must rather be inverted: that existence itself hath corrupted them, even as a stepmother maketh the children unruly. To be set originally, by nature or historical condition, outside the universal — this is the beginning of the demonic, of which the individual is yet not himself guilty. Cumberland's Jew is in this wise also a demon, even though he doth what is good. Thus can the demonic also express itself as contempt for men — a contempt which yet, mark well, doth not bring the demonic himself to act contemptibly; on the contrary, he hath his strength in knowing that he is better than all who judge him. — Concerning all such matters the poet ought first and foremost to raise an alarm. God knoweth what writings the now-living younger versifiers read! Their study consisteth, no doubt, in learning rhymes by heart. — God knoweth what their significance in existence is! At this moment I know not that they do any other use than that they furnish an edifying proof of the soul's immortality, in that one can confidently say of them to oneself what Baggesen saith of the city's poet Kildevalle: if he becometh immortal, then become we all so. — What hath here been said in the matter of Sarah, mainly in the direction of poetic production, and therefore with a fantastic presupposition, hath its full meaning, when one would, with psychological interest, sink into the meaning of the old saying: nullum unquam exstitit magnum ingenium sine aliqua dementia. For this dementia is the genius's suffering in existence — is the expression for, if I dare so put it, the divine envy, while the genial is the expression of preferential love. Thus is the genius from the beginning disoriented in relation to the universal, and brought into relation to the paradox — whether he, in despair over his limitation, which in his eyes transformeth his omnipotence into impotence, seeketh a demonic appeasement, and therefore will not acknowledge it either before God or before men, or whether he religiously calmeth himself in love to the deity. Here lie psychological tasks, on which it seemeth to me one might gladly sacrifice an entire life; and yet so seldom doth one hear a word about them. In what relation doth mental derangement stand to genius? Can one construe the one out of the other? In what sense and how far is the genius master over his derangement? For it followeth of itself that he, to a certain degree, is master over it, since otherwise he were really deranged. To such observations belong, however, shrewdness in a high degree, and love; for to observe the superior is most difficult. If one would, with attention to this, read through some of the most genial authors, then it might still be possible, just very seldom, even with much trouble, to discover a little.

One more case I will think of: that a single individual by being hidden and by his silence wisheth to save the universal. For this I can use the legend of Faust. Faust is a doubter, an apostate of the spirit, who walketh the way of the flesh.

This is the poets' view; and although it is repeated again and again that every age hath its Faust, yet doth one of its poets after another walk unwearied along the well-trodden highway. Let us undertake a little alteration. Faust is the doubter κατ' ἐξοχήν; but he is a sympathetic nature. Even in Goethe's interpretation of Faust I miss a deeper psychological insight into doubt's secret conversations with itself. In our age, when after all everyone hath experienced doubt, no poet hath yet taken a step in this direction. I therefore think also that I might safely offer them royal stationery to write upon, in order to write down all the much that they in this respect have experienced — they would scarcely write more than what could be contained on the foremost margin.

Only when one in this way bendeth Faust into himself, only then can doubt take itself out poetically, only then doth he properly discover, in actuality, all its sufferings. He knoweth then that it is spirit that beareth existence, but he knoweth also that the security and joy in which men live are not grounded in the power of spirit, but easily explainable as unreflected blissfulness. As doubter, as the doubter, he is higher than all this; and if any would deceive him by making him believe that he had passed through doubt, he easily seeth through it; for he who hath made a movement in the world of spirit — that is, an infinite movement — he can straightway

existence. I demand, then, this high-mindedness of him; but if he hath it, dareth he then be silent? Ethics is a dangerous science; and it might well be possible that Aristophanes, determined purely ethically, hath resolved to let laughter pass judgment upon the bewildered age. Aesthetic high-mindedness cannot help; for on that account one ventureth not such a thing. If he is to be silent, then must he enter into the paradox. — One more sketch I will indicate: that, for example, a man possesseth an interpretation of a hero's life, which in a sorrowful way explaineth it, and yet a whole age resteth absolutely securely in this hero, without suspecting any such thing.

hear through the line, whether it be a man of trial that speaketh, or a Munchausen. What a Tamerlane can do with his Huns, that doth Faust know he can do with his doubt — to startle men up in horror, to let existence sway under their feet, to splinter men asunder, to bring the cry of anxiety to sound everywhere. And if he do it, then he is yet no Tamerlane; he is in a certain sense authorized, and hath the authorization of thought. But Faust is a sympathetic nature; he loveth existence; his soul knoweth no envy; he seeth that he cannot stop the raging he can well awaken; he coveteth no Herostratic glory — he is silent; he hideth doubt in his soul more carefully than the maiden who hideth the fruit of a sinful love beneath her heart; he striveth as best he may to keep step with other men, but what goeth on within him he consumeth in himself, and so he bringeth himself as a sacrifice for the universal.

One can sometimes hear men complain when an eccentric head raiseth the whirl of doubt; they say then: would that he had been silent! This idea Faust realizeth. He who hath any conception of what it meaneth that a man liveth by spirit, knoweth also what doubt's hunger meaneth, and that the doubter hungereth as much for life's daily bread as for the nourishment of the spirit. Although then all the pain Faust suffereth may be a quite good argument that it is not pride that hath possessed him, yet I will use a small precautionary measure which I easily devise; for as Gregorius Riminensis was called tortor infantium, because he assumed the damnation of little children, so might I be tempted to call myself: tortor heroum; for I am very inventive when it cometh to torturing the heroes. Faust seeth Margaret — not after he hath chosen lust; for my Faust chooseth not at all lust; he seeth Margaret, not in Mephistopheles's concave mirror, but in all her lovely innocence, and since his soul hath preserved love for men, he can also very well fall in love with her. But he is a doubter; his doubt hath annihilated for him actuality; for so ideal is my Faust that he belongeth not to those scientific doubters who doubt one hour each semester at the lectern, but otherwise can do everything else, just as they do this — without the condition of spirit, or by virtue of spirit. He is a doubter, and the doubter hungereth as much for joy's daily bread as for spirit's food. Yet he remaineth true to his resolve and is silent, and speaketh to no man of his doubt, and to Margaret either of his love.

It followeth of itself that Faust is too ideal a figure to put up with the chatter that, were he to speak, he would occasion a general discussion, or the whole would pass off without consequence, or perhaps, or perhaps. (Here slumbereth, as every poet will easily see, the comic in the sketch — by bringing Faust into an ironic relation to those low-comic fools who in our age run after doubt, who put forth an outward argument that they really have doubted, for example a doctor's certificate, or swear that they have doubted everything, or prove it by the fact that on their journey they fell in with a doubter; these expresses and quick-runners in the world of spirit, who in greatest haste pick up at one man a little inkling of doubt, at another of faith, and now wirthschafte in the best way, just as the parish wisheth fine sand or coarse.) Faust is too ideal a figure to walk in train. He who hath not an infinite passion is not ideal, and he who hath an infinite passion hath long since saved his soul out of such drivel. He is silent in order to sacrifice himself — or he speaketh with the consciousness that he will confuse all things.
If he is silent, then ethics passeth judgment upon him; for it saith:

“Thou shalt acknowledge the universal, and thou acknowledgest it precisely by speaking, and thou darest not have compassion on the universal.” This consideration one ought not to forget, when one occasionally judgeth a doubter strictly, because he speaketh. I am not inclined to judge such conduct mildly; but here, as everywhere, it dependeth upon the movements being made normally. If wrong is to be done, then is a doubter, even though by speaking he brought every possible misfortune upon the world, far to be preferred to those wretched sweet-tooths who taste of everything, and who would heal doubt without knowing it, and who therefore in general are the proximate occasion that doubt breaketh forth wildly and ungovernably. — If he speak, he confoundeth all things; for whether or not it cometh to pass, that learneth he only afterwards, and the outcome can help no one, neither in the moment of action, nor with respect to responsibility.

If he be silent on his own responsibility, then can he indeed act high-mindedly; but to his other pain he will feel a small spiritual trial; for the universal will constantly torment him and say: thou shouldst have spoken; where wilt thou find the certainty that it was not, after all, a hidden pride that governed thy resolve?

If, on the other hand, the doubter can become the single individual who as the single individual standeth in an absolute relation to the absolute, then can he obtain an authorization for his silence. In that case must he make his doubt into guilt. In that case is he in the paradox; but in that case is his doubt healed, even if he might receive another doubt.

Even the New Testament would acknowledge such a silence. There even occur passages in the New Testament which extol irony, only that it is used to hide the better. This movement, however, is just as much that of irony as of any other that hath its ground in this, that subjectivity is higher than actuality. This our age will know nothing of; it will, generally, know nothing more about irony than what Hegel hath said, who, oddly enough, did not understand much of it, and bore it a grudge — which our age hath good grounds not to give up; for it hath but to beware of irony. It is said in the Sermon on the Mount: when thou fastest, anoint thy head and wash thy face, that men may not see that thou fastest. This passage testifieth plainly that subjectivity is incommensurable with actuality, yea, that it hath leave to deceive. If only those folk who in our age go feeling about with loose talk of the idea of the congregation would read the New Testament, then might they perhaps come to other thoughts.

But now Abraham — how acted he? For I have not forgotten, and the reader will now perhaps be pleased to remember, that it was in order to come up against this that I let myself in upon the whole foregoing investigation — not as if Abraham would thereby become more intelligible, but in order that the unintelligibility might become more desultory; for, as I said, Abraham I cannot understand, him I can only admire. It was also remarked that none of the stages described contained an analogy to Abraham; they were only developed so that, while they were exhibited within their own sphere, they might in the moment of misalignment, as it were, indicate the boundary of the unknown land. Insofar as there should be any question of an analogy, it would have to be the paradox of sin; but this lieth again in another sphere, and cannot explain Abraham, and is itself far more easily explained than Abraham.
Abraham, then, did not speak; he spoke not to Sarah, not to Eliezer, not to Isaac; he passed by the three ethical instances; for the ethical had for Abraham no higher expression than family life.
Aesthetics permitted, indeed required, silence of the single individual when by keeping silent he could save another.

This already shows sufficiently that Abraham does not lie within the compass of the aesthetic. His silence is by no means in order to save Isaac, just as in general his whole task — to sacrifice Isaac for his own and for God's sake — is to aesthetics an offense; for aesthetics can well understand that I sacrifice myself, but not that I sacrifice another for my own sake. The aesthetic hero was silent. Ethics, however, judged him because he was silent by virtue of his accidental singularity. It was his human foreknowledge that determined him to be silent. This ethics cannot forgive; every such human knowledge is only an illusion; ethics demands an infinite movement, it demands disclosure. The aesthetic hero, then, can speak, but will not.

The proper tragic hero sacrifices himself and all that is his for the universal; his deed, every stirring within him, belongs to the universal; he is manifest, and in this disclosure ethics' beloved son. This does not fit Abraham; he does nothing for the universal, and he is hidden.

Now, then, we stand at the paradox. Either the single individual as the single individual can stand in an absolute relation to the absolute, and then the ethical is not the highest, or else Abraham is lost: he is neither a tragic hero nor an aesthetic hero.

To this extent it may again seem here that the paradox is the easiest and most convenient of all. Meanwhile, I must repeat that he who holds himself convinced of this is not the knight of faith; for the need and the anxiety are the only justification that can be conceived, even though it cannot be conceived universally — for then the paradox is annulled.

Abraham is silent — but he cannot speak; therein lie the need and the anxiety. For when, even as I am speaking, I cannot make myself understood, then I am not speaking, even though I were to speak uninterruptedly night and day. Such is Abraham's case. He can say everything; but one thing he cannot say, and yet, when he cannot say it — that is, say it in such a way that another understands it — then he does not speak. The relieving thing in speech is that it translates me into the universal. Now Abraham can say the most beautiful things any tongue can muster about how he loves Isaac. But this is not what lies upon his mind; it is the deeper thing — that he wills to sacrifice him because it is a trial. This last no one can understand, and so anyone can only misunderstand the first. This need the tragic hero does not know. He has, in the first place, the consolation that every counter-argument hath had its due — that he hath been able to give Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, Achilles, the chorus, every living being, every voice from the heart of mankind, every cunning, every anxious, every accusing, every compassionate thought the occasion to rise up against him. He can be sure that everything which could be said against him hath been said, ruthlessly, mercilessly — and to strive against the whole world is a consolation, to strive with oneself is dreadful —; he need not fear that he hath overlooked anything, that he must one day afterward perchance cry out, as did King Edward IV at the news of Clarence's murder:
Wer bat für ihn? Wer kniet' in meinem Grimm Zu Füssen mir und bat mich überlegen? Wer sprach von Bruderpflicht? Wer sprach von Liebe?

The tragic hero knows not the dreadful responsibility of solitude. Next, he hath the consolation that he can weep and lament with Clytemnestra and Iphigenia — and tears and cries assuage, but unutterable sighs torture. Agamemnon can quickly gather his soul into the certainty that he will act, and then he hath still time to console and to encourage. This Abraham cannot do. When his heart is moved, when his words would contain a blessed comfort for the whole world, then he dare not console; for would not Sarah, would not Eliezer, would not Isaac say to him: “Why wilt thou then do it? thou canst surely leave it undone.” And if then in his need he would give vent, would embrace all that was dear to him before he proceeded to the last, then he might bring about the dreadful thing, that Sarah, that Eliezer, that Isaac were offended at him and believed him a hypocrite. Speak he cannot, he speaks no human tongue. Even though he himself understood all the tongues of earth, even though the beloved likewise understood them, yet can he not speak — he speaks in a divine tongue, he speaks in tongues.

This need I can well understand, I can admire Abraham, I do not fear that anyone, by reason of this story, should be tempted lightly to wish to be the single individual; but I confess also that I have not the courage for it, and that I gladly renounce every prospect of going further, if only it were possible that I should sometime, however late it might be, come so far. At every moment Abraham can break off, he can repent the whole as a spiritual trial, then he can speak, then all can understand him — but then he is no longer Abraham.

Abraham cannot speak; for that which would explain everything, that it is a trial — and, mark well, such a one wherein the ethical is the temptation — this he cannot say (so that it is intelligible). He who is so situated is an emigrant from the sphere of the universal. But the next thing he can still less say. For Abraham makes, as has earlier been sufficiently developed, two movements. He makes the infinite movement of resignation and gives up Isaac — this no one can understand, since it is a private undertaking; but next he makes at every moment the movement of
faith. This is his consolation. For he says, that is to say:

yet it will not happen, or if it should happen, then the Lord will give me a new Isaac, by virtue, namely, of the absurd. The tragic hero, on the other hand, gets the story to an end. Iphigenia bows under her father's resolve, she herself makes the infinite movement of resignation, and they are now in understanding with one another. She can understand Agamemnon, because his undertaking expresses the universal. Were Agamemnon, on the other hand, to say to her: “Although the god demands thee as a sacrifice, yet were it possible that he did not demand it, by virtue, namely, of the absurd,” — in the same instant he would become unintelligible to Iphigenia. Could he say it by virtue of human calculation, then Iphigenia would surely understand him; but then it would follow that Agamemnon had not made the infinite movement of resignation, and so he is no hero, so the seer's pronouncement is a piece of skipper's gossip, and the whole event a vaudeville.

Abraham, then, did not speak. Only one word of his is preserved, the only line spoken to Isaac, which also sufficiently proves that he had not spoken before. Isaac asks Abraham where the lamb for the burnt offering is. “And Abraham said: God will provide himself the lamb for the burnt offering, my son!”

This last word of Abraham I shall here consider somewhat more closely. Were this word not, then the whole event would lack something; were it otherwise, then everything might perhaps dissolve into confusion.

It hath often been the object of my reflection how far a tragic hero, whether he culminate in a suffering or in an action, ought to have a final line. It depends, so far as I can judge, upon what sphere of life he belongs to, how far his life hath intellectual significance, how far his suffering or action stands in relation to spirit.
It follows of itself that the tragic hero in his

moment of culmination, like every other man who is not bereft of speech, can say a few words, perhaps a few fitting words, but the question is how far it is fitting for him to say them. If the significance of his life lieth in an outward deed, then he hath nothing to say, then all that he saith is essentially mere prattle, whereby he only weakens the impression of himself; whereas the tragic ceremonial bids him in silence accomplish his task, whether this consist in an action or in a suffering. Not to go too far, I will but take what lies nearest at hand. If Agamemnon himself, not Calchas, were to draw the knife against Iphigenia, then he would but have demeaned himself by wishing in the last instant to say a few words; for the meaning of his deed was, after all, evident to all; the procedure of piety, of pity, of feeling, of tears was completed; and otherwise his life had no relation to spirit, that is, he was no teacher, no witness of the spirit. If, on the contrary, the significance of a hero's life is in the direction of spirit, then the lack of a line would weaken the impression of him. What he then hath to say is not a few fitting words, a little declamation-piece, but the meaning of his line is that he carries himself through in the decisive moment. Such an intellectual tragic hero ought to have, and ought to keep, the last word. Of him is required the same transfigured bearing which beseems every tragic hero, but then is required of him one more word. Insofar, then, as such an intellectual tragic hero culminates in a suffering (in death), then in this last word he becomes immortal before he dies, whereas, on the contrary, the ordinary tragic hero only becomes immortal after his death. Socrates one may use as an example. He was an intellectual tragic hero. His death sentence is announced unto him. In that instant he dies, for he who understandeth not that the whole power of the spirit is required in order to die, and that the hero always dieth before he dieth, he shall not come very far in his contemplation of life. As a hero, then, it is required of Socrates that he calmly rest in himself, but as an intellectual tragic hero it is required of him that in this last instant he have spirit-strength enough to carry himself through. He cannot, then, like the ordinary tragic hero, concentrate on holding himself up over against death, but he must so quickly make this movement that in the same instant he is, with his consciousness, beyond this struggle and asserts himself. Were Socrates thus to have fallen silent in the crisis of death, then he would have weakened the effect of his life, awakened a suspicion that the elasticity of irony in him was not a world-power, but a play whose resilience in the decisive moment must be employed by an inverse measure to hold him up pathetically.*

What hath here been briefly intimated cannot indeed find its application to Abraham, insofar as one means by some analogy to discover a fitting word for Abraham wherewith to end; but well insofar as one perceives the necessity that Abraham in the last instant must carry himself through, must not silently draw the knife, but must have a word to say, since as the father of faith he hath absolute significance in the direction of spirit. What he is to say, of that I can form no conception in advance; after he hath said it, then I can well understand, well in a certain sense understand Abraham in the

Which line of Socrates is to be considered the decisive one — about that opinions may be divided, since Socrates hath in so many ways been poetically dispersed by Plato. I propose the following: the death sentence is announced unto him; in the same instant he dies; in the same instant he overcomes death and carries himself through in the famous reply: that it surprised him that he had been condemned by a majority of three votes. With no idle and loose talk in the marketplace, with no foolish remark of an idiot, could he have jested more ironically than with that death sentence which condemneth himself from life.

matter, without thereby having come any nearer to him than I have been to him in the foregoing. Had there existed no last line of Socrates, then I could have thought myself into him and formed such a one; had I not been able to do that, a poet would have been capable of it; but Abraham no poet attaineth.

Before I pass over to a closer consideration of Abraham's last word, I must first call attention to the difficulty that Abraham can come to say anything at all. The need and the anxiety in the paradox lay, as developed above, precisely in the silence — Abraham cannot speak.* To this extent, then, it is a self-contradiction to require that he speak, unless one will have him out again of the paradox in such a way that he in the decisive instant suspends it, whereby he then ceases to be Abraham and annuls the whole foregoing. Were Abraham thus, in the decisive instant, to say to Isaac: it is thou whom this concerns — then this were but a weakness. For could he speak at all, then he must have spoken long ago; and the weakness would lie in this, that he had not had the maturity and concentration of spirit to think the whole pain through beforehand, but had pushed something away from himself, so that the actual pain was a more than the thought one. Besides, by such a speech he would fall out of the paradox, and if he really would speak with Isaac, he must transform his condition into a spiritual trial; for otherwise he could yet say nothing, and if he does this, then he is not even a tragic hero.
Meanwhile a final word of Abraham is yet preserved, and insofar as I can understand the paradox, I can

Insofar as there can be any question of an analogy, the death-situation of Pythagoras affords such a one; for the silence which he had ever maintained he must carry through in his last instant, and therefore he said: it is better to be killed than to speak. Cf. Diogenes, Book 8, §39.

also understand Abraham's total presence in this word. He says, first and foremost, nothing; and in this form he says what he hath to say. His answer to Isaac hath the form of irony, for it is always irony when I say something and yet say nothing. Isaac asks Abraham in the supposition that Abraham is knowing. Were Abraham to have answered: I know nothing — then he had said an untruth. Say something he cannot, for what he knoweth he cannot say. He answers, then: God will provide himself the lamb for the burnt offering, my son! One sees from this the double movement in Abraham's soul, such as it hath been described in the foregoing. Had Abraham merely resigned Isaac and done no more, then he hath said an untruth; for he knoweth, after all, that God demandeth Isaac as a sacrifice, and he knoweth that he himself in this very instant is ready to sacrifice him. He hath then, at every instant, after having made this movement, made the next, made the movement of faith by virtue of the absurd. To this extent he saith no untruth; for by virtue of the absurd it is, after all, possible that God might do something quite otherwise. He saith, then, no untruth, but neither doth he say anything; for he speaketh in a foreign tongue. This becometh yet more evident when we consider that it was Abraham himself who was to sacrifice Isaac. Had the task been a different one, had the Lord commanded Abraham to bring Isaac out upon Mount Moriah, where He himself would let His lightning strike Isaac and so take him as a sacrifice, then Abraham could in the straightforward sense have been right to speak as enigmatically as he doth; for then he could not himself have known what would come to pass. But as the task is set Abraham, he himself shall act, and so he must in the decisive instant know what he himself will do, and consequently he must know that Isaac is to be sacrificed. Hath he not known this with definiteness, then he hath not made the infinite movement of resignation, then his word is indeed no untruth, but at the same time he is very far from being Abraham, he is more insignificant than a tragic hero, yea, he is an irresolute man who can decide neither for the one nor for the other, and who on that account will always come to speak in riddles. But such a hesitator is precisely the parody of the knight of faith.

It shows itself, then, again here, that one can well understand Abraham, but understand him only in such wise as one understands the paradox. I, for my part, can well understand Abraham, but apprehend at the same time that I have not the courage to speak in this manner, just as little as I have the courage to act as Abraham did; but by this I do not in any way say that it is something trivial, since on the contrary it is the only wondrous thing.

And what now did the contemporary age judge of the tragic hero? That he was great, and it admired him. And that venerable assembly of the noble, the jury which every generation constituteth to judge the foregoing generation — it judged likewise. But Abraham, there was no one who could understand. And yet what did he attain? That he remained true to his love. But he who loveth God needeth not tears, not admiration, he forgetteth the suffering in the love, yea, so utterly hath he forgotten it that there should not even afterward be the slightest intimation of his pain, did not God Himself remember it; for He seeth in secret, and knoweth the need, and counteth the tears, and forgetteth nothing.
Either, then, there is a paradox, that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute, or else Abraham is lost.

chapters.title: Epilogue
paragraphs: When once in Holland the prices of spices became somewhat flat, the merchants had a couple of cargoes sunk in the sea, in order to screw up the price. This was a pardonable, perhaps a necessary deception. Is it something similar we have need of in the world of spirit? Are we so thoroughly persuaded that we are come unto the Highest, that there is nothing else left but piously to make ourselves believe that we are not come so far, merely in order to have somewhat with which to fill out the time? Is it such a self-deception the present generation has need of? Is it to a virtuosity in this that it is to be trained? Or is it not rather sufficiently perfected in the art of deceiving itself? Or is what it has need of not rather an honest earnestness which, undaunted and incorruptible, points unto the tasks — an honest earnestness which lovingly fences about the tasks, which doth not affright men into wishing to startle themselves into the Highest, but keepeth the tasks young, and “fair and lovely to behold, and beckoning unto all, and yet withal difficult and inspiring for the noble; for the noble nature is inspired only by that which is difficult.” Whatsoever one generation may learn from another, the properly human no generation learneth from a foregoing one.

In this respect every generation beginneth primitively, hath no other task than every foregoing generation, getteth no further either, in so far as the foregoing did not betray the task and deceive itself. This properly human is passion, wherein also the one generation perfectly understandeth the other and understandeth itself. Thus to love hath no generation learned from another; no generation cometh to begin at any other point than at the beginning; no later generation hath a shorter task than the foregoing; and if a man here will not, like the foregoing generations, abide by loving, but go further — then this is but an idle and foolish discourse.

But the highest passion in a man is faith, and no generation here beginneth at any other point than the foregoing; every generation beginneth from the beginning; the succeeding generation getteth no further than the foregoing, in so far as that one held its task in trust and did not leave it in the lurch. That this should be wearisome is naturally somewhat the generation cannot say; for the generation hath, after all, the task, and hath nothing to do with the matter that the foregoing generation had the same task — unless the individual generation, or the individuals in the generation, presumptuously will take that place which belongeth only to the Spirit which ruleth the world, and which hath patience not to grow weary. If the generation begin upon such a thing, then is it perverse, and what wonder then that the whole of existence seemeth perverse to it; for surely there is no one who hath found existence more perverse than that tailor who, according to the fairy-tale, came up alive into heaven and from this vantage looked down upon the world. So soon as the generation concerneth itself only with its task, which is the Highest, then can it not grow weary; for the task is always sufficient for a man's life. When children upon a holiday have already, ere twelve of the clock, played through all their games, and now impatiently say: Is there none then who can think up a new game? — doth this prove that these children are more developed and more forward than those children in the same age or in a past generation, who could let the well-known games suffice for the whole day? Or doth it not rather prove that those first children lack what I would call the lovely earnestness which belongeth unto play?

Faith is the highest passion in a man. There are perhaps in every generation many who do not even come unto it, but none cometh further. Whether also in our age there are many who do not discover it, I do not determine; I dare only appeal to myself, who do not conceal that for him there are long prospects, without that he therefore wisheth to deceive himself or the great by making this into a triviality, into a childhood ailment which one must as soon as possible wish overcome. But even for him who doth not so much as come unto faith, life hath tasks enough, and when he loveth these honestly, then shall his life also not be wasted, even though it never become like the lives of those who perceived and laid hold upon the Highest. But he who came unto faith (be he the eminently gifted or the simple, this maketh nothing to the case) — he doth not stop at faith; nay, he would be indignant if any said it unto him, even as the lover would be enraged were one to say that he stopped at love; for, he would answer, by no means do I stop, since I have my life therein. Yet doth he get no further either, not unto anything else; for when he discovereth this, then hath he another explanation.

“One must go further; one must go further.” This urge to go further is old in the world. The dark Heraclitus, who deposited his thoughts in his writings and his writings in the temple of Diana (for his thoughts had been his armor in life, and therefore he hung it up in the temple of the god) — the dark Heraclitus hath said: one cannot pass twice through the same

river*). The dark Heraclitus had a disciple, who did not abide by this, but went further, and added: one cannot do it even once**). Poor Heraclitus, to have such a disciple! By this improvement the Heraclitean proposition was improved into an Eleatic proposition, which denieth motion; and yet that disciple wished only to be a disciple of Heraclitus, who went further — not back to that which Heraclitus had abandoned.
